items.body: In the digital era, it’s rare to encounter a project as ambitious as this: a triple-LP concept album available as a boxed set, including a book with a short story (in Italian) and 180 illustrations. Un Sequestro Lungo 10,000 Anni is the love child of Samuele Gottardello (Blak Saagan) and Iranian illustrator Majid Bita, the second in a series of Opale Editions by Maple Death Records and Canicola Edizioni. The concept is dystopian, the illustrations vibrant despite their dual tones, portraying a world overrun by monsters and monstrous humans, a savage police force keeping a terrified and often angry populace at bay. In one scene, a bus rushes headlong toward a gaping maw. The apartments are jammed and often infested; Big Brother is everywhere, sharing the sky with the invading beasts. Helicopters roar and crash outside, while some citizens curl into balls and others smoke cigarettes, impassively observing the carnage. An informant uses a dial-up phone; a cleric mourns a fallen world. Angels and devils abound. Yet even amid the flames, there is room for art: writers and illustrators are hard at work, chronicling the chaos. The book’s final sentence: “Start dreaming again.” Given the artist’s background, it’s impossible to ignore the parallels with the current devestation in Iran: set upon from every angle, the populace is at the mercy of bombs from above and repression from below. And yet, this stark combination of dangers can rear its ugly head in any nation. While it’s tempting to think of the album as a dystopian vision (thanks to the presence of skyscraper-tall monsters), its visual metaphors can be applied to the present day. The rough translation: A 10,000 Year Long Kidnapping. Blak Saagan follows first a trajectory, and then an arc. The album begins with electronic music that segues gently into an ambient phase before toppling into rock and jazz and returning to the electronic. A few tracks contain vocals, but an entire LP side worth of material passes before the first words appear. An affection for 80s synth permeates the electronic pieces, conjuring associations with horror films; but while opener “The Blak Fire” is nearly industrial, the closer is as bright as the hopeful denouement. The early electronic pieces are metallic, propulsive and exciting, scoring what might be the initial invasion or the conflict already in progress; there will be time to slow down later, as people choose between the classic options: run, hide, die. “Everything will be swept away,” sings Julinko. Guitars surge like growling behemoths; drums pound like wide Kaiju feet. But by “Henran” (“Bewildered”), it all slows to a quiet boil, saxophone swelling as it struggles to take in a series of incomprehensible vistas. Time begins to distend; four of the final six tracks stretch past the ten minute mark. After the end, there is no more need for watches. The industrial timbres return in “FRREPa (featuring Liz Van Der Nüll)” ~ the sound of resistance re-awakening. The album’s shortest piece at 2:41, it packs the most powerful punch. At the beginning of the next piece, one can hear sirens and the sounds of street protest; the populace has awakened, and the revolution has begun. Midway through the piece, the BPMs increase along with the confidence of the movement. “Disintegrazione” offers a final pause for reflection before the completion of the arc, representing restoration. Such things have happened in history, which means they can happen again; but as this album warns, things may get a whole lot worse before they begin to improve. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Review by canadianeurysm — Where do I begin with The Whirlwind. Possibly the longest Epic ever created by a strong lineup. Everything about the people behind thispiece would suggest it would be outstanding.Mike Portnoy, Ronie Stolt, Pet Trewavas, and Neal Morse (More on the last member later).The song has great pace, and unlike a lot of modern prog it doesn't fall into sounding like a cloneof one of the heavy hitters of the genre (ELP, Yes, Genesis, King Crimson, etc.) - A lot of"smaller" prog bands draw a ton of inspiration from these guys and end up just sounding like a sidegrade. But not Transatlantic (and probably because individually these artists are from big bandsthemselves), there's certainly parallels with some crunchy movements like ELP and the Grandiosemovements like Yes, but still the band manages to maintain its own sound. It's got symphonic bits,ballad bits, even some neo-prog bits. Really something for everyone in the genre. The concept of The Whirlwind is all about the turbulence and struggles of life (like aWhirlwind).... but there's something in the eye of that Whirlwind to make it all good...And that something? It's Jesus. Unfortunately. Neal Morse has a bit of a track record for insertinghis beliefs into his music (as all artists do), but Neal does it in a very cheesy way. At the end of60 minutes of pretty solid prog rock (but not the strongest lyrics) we're greeted with a cheesyChristian Pop Rock 12 minute movement that's musically quite weak compared to the rest of the songand lyrically fairly cringe worthy. The Album overall has some religious motifs and undertones - and in general this is common in music- there's many biblical references across the Prog Rock Genre in some of the greatest works of alltime (Like Genesis' Suppers Ready), but Neal Morse unfortunately approaches this topic with zerotact - and to me, it spoils the entire album. This wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't the end of the song, all the build up and all that work just toend on what feels like a pushy, overly preachy pop-rock song about Neal's faith. If the final movement was in the middle of the song it'd seem out of place but wouldn't be tooegregious, but ending off the entire song undermines the whole Epic.

Their sole album appeared in the second half of the70's, but only completed or released in the mid-90's; and was rather short (30') by internationalstandards, but a fairly professional-sounding affair. One can think of a few classicUS/UK groupslike Yes, but the sextet featured the violin in the forefront, which can make you think more ofKansas or Richardson-era Caravan. However, the vocals are sung in Portuguese, which distinguishesthem semi-immediately (large parts of their music is instrumental); The album starts a bit with a liturgical ambiance before going grandiose & verbose with the albumlongest (8-mins) eponymous track, alternating between all-out rock and symphonic passages. The restof the album follows suit, though as newer tracks flow out of your Hi-Fi, less excitement from thesonwriting pours out. Viana's violin overpowers a lot of the music, except for the bass player, andthe odd piano romantic interludes. If you enjoy Kansas' music, this is in the same vein, but with anaxxentuated violin. Very interesting and happy to have known about this band in the last 30 years,but I wouldn't consider Saecula Saeculorum anything essential listening. So 3.5 stars really!!!

items.body: Review by HogweedOfTuscany — Actually, I am torn with regards to rating this album. For the top rating, the five stars, says "Essential: a masterpiece of progressive music". Ritchie Blackmore's Rainbow is not a masterpiece of progressive music, for it is not an example of "progressive music", really. It is a stellar example of "Elizabethan hard rock music", which is certainly a thing to consider, but taking that as "prog" would take my general tendencies of prog-folk-pastoral-renaissance-whatever crossover way too far. And yet. Prior to listening to this album, decades ago, I had no expectations. Rainbow was the band Blackmore started after leaving Purple, and I was thinking it's going to be your typical vanity project, a lot of guitar, way less sense. And boy, was I surprised. I can't really understate this - even compared to other hard rock albums I had heard by the time I first put on this record (I was probably fourteen, but I had been listening to rock for three solid years of active, voracious listening), Rainbow's debut stands out. EVERY song here makes sense. Every one is catchy, each and every one shows a different approach towards the hard rock paradigm. Even the two main ballads - Catch the Rainbow and Temple of the King - are completely different, the former being a melancholic, intimate tune whereas the latter is the nostalgic, solemn remembrance of things past. Also, I don't think Blackmore - the man behind Burn or Smoke on the Water - ever wrote anything better than the main stomping riff of Man on the Silver Moutain (and the arpeggios in the prechorus). Some say the approach would be perfected on Rising (I don't know, that one is a tad too uneven for me as an album), but even if that was the case, the blueprint is here - and like it or not, Dio has been more or less going to this exact well for the rest of his career.The album still sounds fresh after all these years. It stills sets the bar for "rock" for me, even in the aspect of general album consistency (where it dwarfs even Zeppelin, for example). Not a masterpiece of progressive music, but a masterpiece of rock music, deserving every star it gets.

items.body: Review by ralphabet — October were a progressive rock band from Michigan who produced two privately-pressed albums c. 1979, both of which have become quite sought-after (especially since neither have seen an official reissue of any kind).I find this album a bit tricky to outright recommend, as there are some considerable flaws present. First of all, the production is extremely amateurish and frankly kind of bad. Everything is quite murky and a lot of the instruments lack much of an impact, which is particularly evident on the rhythm section. It's also let down by some weak singing (the intro to "Nero" being particularly egregious and borderline incomprehensible) on the few tracks with vocals.That being said, there's enough interesting ideas that I've relistened to this album multiple times, and I'm always surprised by how much I like it. I think the October albums are too obscure to have any kind of real "consensus" as to which of the two is better, but between this and After The Fall, this is by far my favourite. There's a playful, kind of jazzy undercurrent to many of the songs that I really like, further accentuated by the violin playing (which is the highlight of many tracks here).I don't know; the more I listen to this, the more grows on me. From an objective perspective this isn't really that great or anything, but if you find underground prog and private prog releases interesting, it'll probably be enjoyable for you. You can find better albums out there, but you can also do a lot worse than this.

A Jethro Tull-esque hard rock section follows, featuring constantly shifting drum rhythms; by the time "Gorąca Linia" begins, the bass takes the lead, eventually yielding the spotlight to the piano. Oskar Cenkier shines here, playing with subtlety and holding his own against the persistent progressive hard rock guitar, from which a luminous melody eventually emerges."Pleonasm" soon reveals its deeply jazz-infused essence; Fren momentarily transforms into a trio where bass, drums, and piano become one, at times whispering, at others raising their voices. The moments when the melody slows down only serve to enhance the composition and its varied nuances; it is a pleasure to witness such diversity and the effective use of silence.When the guitar joins in, it does so within that same jazz framework; the rehearsed melodic lines are echoed by the piano before the group moves beyond improvisation to tackle a complex, progressive structure. The soul of "Pleonasm", and that of Fren itself, resides in both these phases. There are contrapuntal exchanges, first by the guitar, then the piano, later the drums, and finally the entire ensemble. The composition is clearly well-crafted, a fact that becomes increasingly apparent with repeated listening as the logic behind each section and its progression reveals itself. Another guitar riff of Balkan origin takes over, and its violence and fire are quelled by droplets of w�ter, which are, in fact, piano notes."Heavy Matter" weaves a symphony where the Mellotron and synthesizer vie to elevate the track, eventually giving way to a guitar-and-piano duet; together, they craft overlapping figures that build a complex melody, another fine composition that knows exactly when to pause and when to resume. "Time to Take Stones Away" recaptures some of that epic, yet unpretentious, Pink Floyd atmosphere found earlier on the album, aided by the guitar... though, as happens throughout the record, the piano disrupts those plans, to the listener's benefit, by introducing classical scalar runs reminiscent of the finale of Rick Wakeman's The Myths and Legends of King Arthur. Yet, the track never loses that symphonic-rock vibe, even as the melodies break free from convention to turn experimental during the trio sections. There are also echoes of the almost folk-like melodies found in the work of Keith Jarrett, Jack DeJohnette, and Gary Peacock, elements woven into the very fabric of the band's symphonic sound.

items.body: All I know is that when I’m with you all the lines they seem to blur I meant it when I said we were through But my heart isn’t so sure MODISTE could have built Nothing More Than a Machine inside a laptop, but the Louisville trio instead surrounds itself with analogue synthesizers, drum machines, and digital instruments from the 80s and 90s – machines with temperaments, imperfect memories, and knobs that invite somebody to reach out and make a decision. “Using these old machines is a small personal rebellion against convenience culture and all the small ways technology is sterilizing the creative process. Also, they’re just more fun. They’re unpredictable and wobbly and alive and have a certain warmth and texture that you just can’t replicate,” vocalist Sydney Sleadd says. Those influences are easy enough to hear. Depeche Mode, Siouxsie and the Banshees, Book of Love, New Order, Metric, The Motels, Tennis, Weyes Blood, and Strange Boutique all provide useful coordinates at different moments, although MODISTE’s strongest songs are the ones where those references begin to blur together. Sleadd’s voice supplies a recognizable center, Stein approaches synthesizers with the curiosity of someone who enjoys their peculiarities, and Stallings introduces enough guitar to keep the electronic arrangements physically grounded. That sense of play gives the album much of its character. Nightmare opens as though the closing credits of a 1987 prime-time drama have suddenly become an invitation, with broad synthesizer chords, bright melodic flourishes, and the faint suggestion that something romantic and vaguely dangerous is waiting around the next corner. As an instrumental, it establishes the album’s affection for period equipment without turning the record into an exercise in museum preservation. There is too much movement in the arrangement, and too much pleasure in the tones themselves, for that. Breaking My Own Heart brings Sleadd forward with a song about the exhausting arithmetic of wanting somebody who disappears whenever intimacy becomes possible. The verses maintain a cool exterior while the chorus gives her considerably more room, allowing the vocal to stretch across the arrangement as frustration turns into self-preservation. Beneath her, the electronics maintain an elegant tension between pop immediacy and emotional unease. The song understands how desire can survive well beyond the point at which common sense has packed its bags. On Blur, Dennis Stein’s synthesizers rise and recede while Kyle Stallings sends guitar through the open spaces, leaving Sleadd room to sing with poise, attraction, and wary self-knowledge. “We wanted Blur to have this ebb and flow that tapped into the feeling of not being able to pull away even when something isn’t good for you,” says Sleadd. The arrangement follows that idea closely. Synth lines swell and withdraw, the guitar adds an occasional flash of abrasion, and Sleadd sounds increasingly aware that recognition offers very little protection against repetition. The chorus catches the contradiction beautifully, with certainty dissolving beneath attraction. My Love heads into power-ballad territory with complete confidence. Sleadd leans into the emotional scale of the song, while the arrangement allows the chords to widen around her rather than crowding every available space. Its euphoric bridge provides one of the album’s most openly romantic moments, the kind of passage designed for a singer to look toward the back of the room and hold the note a little longer than expected. The instrumental Nightmare Part 2 then clears the air. Its spacious electronic architecture brings Jean-Michel Jarre to mind, particularly in the way melody and atmosphere are allowed to develop patiently across repeating figures. Where the opening Nightmare feels connected to television themes and eighties synth-pop drama, its sequel reaches toward something more expansive and cinematic, giving the album a useful midpoint before the songs return to their various romantic complications. Shadows finds MODISTE at its most theatrical. “Shadows delves into themes of longing, forbidden love, repressed desire, and surrender,” says Sleadd. “We wanted it to feel like a slow descent, similar to giving into temptation, with the synths and rhythm building a kind of hypnotic gravity around the words.” The song carries that descent in its pacing. Sleadd sings as though every warning has already been received, considered, and quietly placed to one side. Desire becomes a question of reputation, restraint, and the private thrill of crossing a line while knowing precisely where it was drawn. Shame gets powdered, perfumed, and sent onto the dance floor with a couple of spritzes of Tabu. Beneath the drama, the band keeps a firm hand on the arrangement, allowing the tension to accumulate without burying the lyric beneath excess. Age of the Andy brings one of the record’s strongest rhythmic turns, with a backbeat that carries some of Depeche Mode’s physical economy while Sleadd delivers one of her most assured performances. The keyboards have a harder edge here, and Stallings’ guitar adds pressure around the beat rather than competing with it. The result suits MODISTE particularly well: stylish, muscular synth-pop with enough space for the vocal personality to remain at the center. Besotted returns to the scale of a power ballad, though its emotional engine is a struggle over desire and control. Sleadd understands that these songs become more interesting when love comes with leverage, pride, hesitation, and the possibility of somebody losing the upper hand. The larger arrangement gives those tensions room to breathe, making the track feel less like a declaration than an extended negotiation between two people who know exactly how much power attraction can surrender. “In creating this record, we really discovered how well we worked together and how much we enjoy working together. We’re each pulling from different influences but there’s an overarching shared vision that is the glue of this project,” Stallings says. Listen to Nothing More Than a Machine below, and order the album here. Nothing More Than A Machine by MODISTE Their ambitions extend to the stage. “We’re really trying to create a full experience at our live show that allows everyone, including us, a reprieve from the day to day grind. While it’s a lot of work to pack out these big TVs, lights, and all of our stage production, it’s worth it to build an immersive world for people to come live in for a night,” Stein says. Nothing More Than a Machine earns its title through an affectionate contradiction. MODISTE loves machines because they can misbehave, drift, surprise, and require touch. Across the album, those machines become partners in songs about people behaving much the same way: losing control, guarding themselves badly, making familiar mistakes, and occasionally finding something beautiful in the trouble. items.body: We spend our lives never touching the trauma that we face, I never been proud but I take pride in knowing we radiate our darkest days The comfort that night gave us, as droplets from the rain remind us what we gain There is something almost perverse about how good Nocturnal Prose sounds while contemplating a world that seems determined to grind everybody into administrative paste. Droplets From The Rain, the second single from the San Antonio band’s debut album Western Interests, takes guitars built for nervous pacing, a rhythm section with the precision of a factory press, and Yole Centeno’s exhausted baritone, then points the entire apparatus toward memory: friends, trains, rain, trauma, survival, and those nights when misery somehow became bearable because somebody else was there. Centeno formed Nocturnal Prose after leaving screamo outfit Amygdala, and you can hear the residue of that background beneath the post-punk architecture. The emotional stakes remain high, although the delivery has cooled into something more drained and watchful. His voice sits low in the mix with the weary authority of someone reading the morning headlines after already knowing they will be terrible. Around him, guitarist Nick turns anxiety into movement, stretching chords until they seem ready to split, while bassist Aaron and drummer Chuy lock together so tightly that separating their contributions becomes almost beside the point. You can hear traces of classic 80s post-punk’s vocabulary throughout Droplets From The Rain: the wiry tension, basslines carrying their own emotional burden, and guitars equally capable of abrasion and sudden beauty. There is some of Asylum Party’s wounded romanticism in its atmosphere, while Red Lorry Yellow Lorry and Blitz can be felt in the harder rhythmic edges. Lowlife and For Against hover around the song’s deeper tonal spaces, where the bass does as much emotional work as the voice. Nick’s guitar, meanwhile, reaches toward the expansive playing associated with Chameleons and The Church, continually changing the emotional temperature rather than settling into one repeated figure. Chords stretch outward, smaller phrases scratch nervously around the verses, and eventually the instrument seems to break free of the song’s accumulated anxiety. Droplets From The Rain has enough personality to avoid becoming an archaeological dig through somebody’s record collection. The lyrics detail memories of companionship as a survival mechanism, with passing trains and rainfall functioning as the incidental music of people trying to keep each other alive. There is tenderness, but nobody is selling recovery as a motivational poster. Trauma remains avoided, carried, inherited, and occasionally transformed into pride because getting through a terrible period with another person can become its own small victory; the song carries some of Blade Runner’s rain-streaked finality. Droplets From The Rain shows that despair can have a bassline, memory can have momentum, and friendship can become a form of resistance. The song keeps moving because standing still would mean getting swallowed. By the time the final guitar line recedes, the comfort promised in the title feels provisional, fragile, and necessary. For a band staring straight at modern misery, that measure of grace feels enormous. Nocturnal Prose write from an America saturated with institutional violence, economic exhaustion, ICE raids and detainments, mass distraction, and the daily horror transmitted from Gaza through the same devices used to order dinner. Their response is deeply personal without shrinking into private misery. Listen to Droplets From The Rain below and order the album here. items.body: UK black metal festival Fortress Festival has confirmed a new batch of artists for its dungeon synth stage, which expands to two full days in the theatre room at Scarborough Spa for the event’s fifth anniversary. Fortress Festival 2027 takes place on 29-30 May 2027 in Scarborough, North Yorkshire, UK. Organizers said around 150 tickets remained for the two-day event as of the August 4, 2026 announcement. Leading the new dungeon synth stage confirmations is the worldwide live debut of French dungeon synth artist Erang. Discussing the decision to perform live for the first time, Erang stated: “This music is all my life, and I give everything I have to it. For the longest time, it has been such a solitary thing to craft. 2027 will mark the 15th anniversary of my first album, TOME I, and for the first time, I’ve decided to create a live performance around the Land of the Five Seasons. Because the people who enjoy my music have been asking for this for so many years, and their support is the only thing that matters to me: the Kingdom is Ours!” Dungeon synth stage lineup for Fortress Festival 2027 The dungeon synth stage additions announced on August 4, 2026 are: Erang (France) – worldwide live debut Wraith Knight (US) – UK debut and exclusive performance Spectral Castle (France) – live debut Hole Dweller (US) Atlantean Sword – had to cancel its planned 2026 appearance Lord Bakartia (Spain) DragonKeep (France) These artists join Fortress Festival’s dungeon synth stage alongside the festival’s already-announced main and Ocean Room bills, which are led by Norwegian black metal act Emperor in an exclusive UK headline performance. About Fortress Festival Fortress Festival is a black metal festival held at Scarborough Spa in Scarborough, North Yorkshire, UK. Its first edition ran over three days starting June 2, 2023, and the festival has continued annually since, with its 2025 edition selling out. The 2027 edition, spanning 29-30 May 2027, marks the festival’s fifth anniversary and is organized in partnership with Reaper Agency UK. Fortress Festival’s dungeon synth stage has grown alongside the wider bill, and the 2027 edition expands the format to two consecutive days in the venue’s theatre room. Dungeon synth itself traces back to the early 1990s as an offshoot of black metal, built around synthesizer-led, atmospheric, fantasy-themed soundscapes; Erang, one of the fifth-anniversary stage’s new confirmations, has been part of that scene’s revival since releasing his debut album “TOME I” in 2012.

items.body: Here’s a news that only reached us now. Death By Love released “In Unity (Wieloryb Remix and Tribute)” on 14 July 2026, a two-track single on Distortion Productions built around remixes by the late Polish industrial artist Wieloryb (Paweł Kmiecik), who died in June 2026. The release reworks “In Unity”, a track from the duo’s 2026 debut album “444”, and all profits go to support Kmiecik’s family. In Unity (WIELORYB Remix and Tribute) by Death By Love Death By Love bring a gothic-industrial and darkwave sound that mixes trip-hop pacing with Middle Eastern melodic elements, heard across their debut album “444”. “In Unity” was originally written by Inga Habiba and Peter Guellard for that record. For this release Wieloryb reworked the track into two versions: “In Unity (Wieloryb Vs. Psychotribe Remix)”, edited by Peter Guellard under his Psychotribe alias, and “In Unity (Wieloryb Power Noise Remix)”. Inga Habiba’s vocals carry over from the original, Guellard handled mastering, and Grindhouse Alternative Art Studio created the cover art. Wieloryb also directed the video for the Psychotribe remix before his death, released via Distortion Productions. Peter Guellard explained why the duo dedicated the release to Wieloryb: “We dedicate this release to Wieloryb, Pawel Kmiecik, an extraordinary artist, producer, and video creator, whose vision left a lasting mark on the industrial scene. ‘In Unity’ was the final remix he completed before his sudden and unexpected passing. His post-apocalyptic industrial landscapes sent chills down our spines, while his relentless rhythms and crushing soundscapes raised our pulse and demanded movement. His work was raw, uncompromising, and unforgettable. Thank you for everything Pawel. Your legacy lives on through the art you left behind. All profits from this release will go directly to support Pawel’s family.” The video for “In Unity (Wieloryb Vs. Psychotribe Remix)” is on YouTube. Wieloryb, the artist behind ‘In Unity’ Wieloryb was the project of Paweł Kmiecik, formed in 1994 in Poland’s Trójmiasto area (Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) and among the country’s earliest EBM acts. Its debut cassette, “1”, earned a nomination for the Fryderyk award, Poland’s main music industry prize, and the project went on to blend electro-industrial, EBM and techno with noise, metallic rhythms and ambient textures across releases including “2”, “3” and, in 2025, “No Flag” on Requiem Records. Side-Line interviewed Kmiecik about “No Flag” in January 2026, months before his death. About Death By Love Death By Love is a Polish-U.S. dark electronic duo formed by Polish singer-songwriter Inga Habiba and Polish-born, U.S.-based producer and multi-instrumentalist Peter Guellard, whose past work includes the Polish goth band Blitzkrieg and the U.S. dark-electronic underground. The pair’s collaboration grew out of a remix Guellard made for Habiba’s electronic act NUN Electro, which led to further work on her solo project CallMe and, eventually, to Death By Love. The duo signed to Distortion Productions in January 2025 and released their debut single, “Strong Inside”, the same month, followed by a cover of Maanam’s “Krakowski Spleen” in March 2025. Their debut album, “444”, followed on Distortion Productions in February 2026: an 11-track record combining gothic, industrial and trip-hop elements with Middle Eastern melodic touches, exploring mysticism, identity and spiritual tension. Its tracks include “Sellenno”, “Cosmic Power”, “In Unity” and “Temros (Symphonic Mix)”, a reworked version of a track that first appeared on the compilation “Electronic Saviors Vol. 7: ReUnion”. “In Unity (WIELORYB Remix and Tribute)”, released on 14 July 2026, reworks the album’s “In Unity” into two Wieloryb remixes and doubles as a tribute to the Polish industrial artist.

items.body: Chicago electronic trio Pixel Grip has announced ‘Percepticide: Remixed’, a remix package built from their 2025 album “Percepticide: The Death of Reality.” The self-released project rolls out on Bandcamp, opened by Glasgow-based producer KAVARI’s rework of the album track “Noise,” released July 10, 2026, with the wider package following on July 29, 2026. Noise (KAVARI Remix) by Pixel Grip ‘Percepticide: Remixed’ tracklist and contributors “Percepticide: The Death of Reality,” released independently on June 12, 2025, was Pixel Grip’s third studio album and first fully self-released record, running twelve tracks: “Crows Feast,” “Bet You Do.,” “Stamina,” “Reason to Stay,” “Insignificant,” “Noise,” “Moment with God,” “Split,” “Last Laugh,” “Work or Shut Up,” “Jealousy is Lethal” and “Gonna Be Faster.” For “Percepticide: Remixed,” each of those tracks is reworked by a different producer, with some, including “Reason to Stay,” receiving multiple versions. Confirmed contributors include KAVARI, Perel, Curses, Auragraph, Frazer Ray, Matrixxman, Mercy Girl, Fire-Toolz, Black Asteroid, Inhalt, club.drippy, A Thousand Mad Things, Majick, Ole Mic Odd and Normal Bias, alongside a Pixel Grip self-remix. KAVARI’s version of “Noise” reworks the original into a harder club arrangement. Pixel Grip is Rita Lukea on vocals with Tyler Ommen and Jonathon Freund handling production, active since 2018. Earlier in 2026, the band contributed a remix of Nine Inch Nails’ “As Alive as You Need Me to Be” to the compilation “TRON Ares: Divergence”, released alongside contributions from Mark Pritchard, Boys Noize, Lanark Artefax, Chilly Gonzales and other artists. No CD or vinyl edition of “Percepticide: Remixed” has been announced; the release is confirmed for digital release via Bandcamp only. About Pixel Grip Pixel Grip formed in Chicago, Illinois, in 2018, built around vocalist Rita Lukea with producers Tyler Ommen and Jonathon Freund. The trio’s sound draws on electropop, darkwave, minimal synth, coldwave and EBM, shaped in part by Chicago’s queer club and disco scenes. The band released its debut album, “Heavy Handed,” in 2019, followed by “Arena” in 2021. “Percepticide: The Death of Reality” arrived on June 12, 2025, as Pixel Grip’s third studio album and its first release without a label, described by the band as a record built around betrayal, trauma, rage and reconstruction. In February 2026, Pixel Grip contributed a remix to “TRON Ares: Divergence,” the various-artists companion project featuring new material from Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross alongside Nine Inch Nails. With “Percepticide: Remixed,” Pixel Grip extends the “Percepticide” era into a second, fully collaborative release, handing the original album over to a wide field of electronic producers for reinterpretation.

items.body: Swedish electronic act Twice a Man will release “The Marine Trilogy”, a 48-page 2CD artbook compiling out-of-print, marine-themed material recorded between 1984 and 1986, on October 23, 2026 through Dependent, limited to 500 copies. Twice a Man’s ‘The Marine Trilogy’ artbook The tracks originally appeared on the cassette “Waterland” and the 12″ singles “Aqua Marine Drum” and “Across The Ocean,” releases that have since become sought-after collectors’ items. “The Marine Trilogy” gathers and remasters that material for its first appearance on CD. Pre-sale for the artbook begins September 9, 2026. The band describes “Waterland” as the result of a collaboration with the Center for Studies of Whales and Dolphins, which recorded the whale sounds used as the bassline on “Across the Ocean.” Twice a Man frame the material around the marine world as “a perspective from which to view the world,” made amid what the band calls its “fear of the turbulent world order” of the mid-1980s. The group also confirmed a new full-length album is in the works, to be announced separately. About Twice a Man Twice a Man is a Swedish electronic duo from Gothenburg, formed by Dan Söderqvist and Karl Gasleben (born Ingemar Ljungström), who met in the early 1970s playing in the groups Älgarnas Trädgård and Anna Själv Tredje. The pair started working together in 1978 as Cosmic Overdose, renamed the project Twice a Man in 1981 and released their debut album, “Music For Girls,” in 1982. From 1984 the group began incorporating samplers into its synthesizer-based, theatrical sound, a period that produced the marine-themed “Waterland” cassette and the “Aqua Marine Drum” and “Across The Ocean” singles now collected on “The Marine Trilogy.” Long-time collaborator Jocke Söderqvist rejoined the group in 2013. More recently, Twice a Man released the video for “Dahlia” in 2023, remastered former member Lars Falk’s classic 1980s-era material, and in 2025 announced the album “The Coloured Breeze Is a New Dimension,” led by the single “Birds Eye View.” “The Marine Trilogy,” due October 23, 2026, revisits the band’s mid-1980s marine-themed recordings ahead of a new full-length album still to be announced.

items.body: Tender Ender, the solo project of Swiss artist Thomas Schmidiger, released the single “Darkness”, accompanied by a self-directed music video, ahead of his second album, “Red Kites”, due November 13, 2026. The single is also available to stream via iMusician. Tender Ender’s ‘Darkness’ single and ‘Red Kites’ album “Darkness” is built around a home organ and its built-in rhythm section, a duet pairing Schmidiger’s baritone with the breathy vocals of Sabine Ruch. Schmidiger describes the track as “a living-room-sized hymn,” where the home organ “rolls out the carpet for a soothing daydream of escape,” and compares its mood to dark chocolate: “bittersweet, velvety and uplifting.” Schmidiger also directed the accompanying video, shot during the annual wheat harvest and the swarms of red kites that gather over the fields afterward. He explains the imagery came to him ready-made: “It was basically ready-made,” he says of the harvest and the birds, adding that the scene “somehow summed it all up.” “I like boring things,” he says. “They tend to open doors you didn’t even know existed.” “Darkness” is the first single from “Red Kites”, out November 13, 2026 and available to preorder on Tender Ender’s site. About Tender Ender Tender Ender is the solo project of Swiss artist Thomas Schmidiger, blending film-noir pop, ambient melancholy and piano balladry built around a home organ, enriched with harmonium, vibraphone, pedal steel and piano. Less than a year after his debut album, Schmidiger returns with “Red Kites”, due November 13, 2026, led by the single “Darkness” featuring vocalist Sabine Ruch.

items.body: Danish electropop act deZeption releases the single “Am I You” on August 7, 2026, through Town And Towers Records. Town And Towers describes “Am I You” as a single that “blends infectious electronic rhythms, lush soundscapes, and thought-provoking lyrics about identity, humanity, and artificial intelligence.” The release is the latest step in deZeption’s ongoing work as a solo project of Jan Brink, who is currently writing material for the band’s third album; “Am I You” is not confirmed as part of that album at this stage. deZeption pairs ‘Am I You’ with a ‘Human Eyes’ vinyl reissue Alongside the new single, deZeption’s 2008 debut album “Human Eyes” is reissued on 12″ vinyl, available through Elastic Stage. “Human Eyes” was originally self-released on CDr in 2008 on deZeption’s own deZeptivemusic label and was positively received in Denmark, Germany and Norway; Town And Towers reissued the ten-track album digitally in September 2024, and the new vinyl edition follows that reissue. Human Eyes by deZeption About deZeption deZeption was formed in Denmark in May 2003 as a part-time project by Jan Brink and Claus Lindeskov Hansen. The duo’s debut album, “Human Eyes”, followed in 2008 on their own deZeptivemusic label and was positively received in Denmark, Germany and Norway, leading to concerts in all three countries. Kim B. Sommer joined as a live keyboard player in May 2005 and was subsequently made a permanent member; he later left to form the band Synthnoter. Lead singer Claus Lindeskov Hansen left deZeption in August 2011 and later revived his music under the name enter.me. Henning Wibrand joined as deZeption’s new lead singer in July 2012. The band’s second album, “Mature”, followed in 2017, alongside a music video for the track “While the Wind Blows”; Kim B. Sommer left the band the same year and went on to join Synthnoter. This “new” deZeption line-up played its live debut in 2018, and Jan Brink and Henning Wibrand ended their collaboration in October 2019. Morten Kristensen of the Danish electropop act Disrupted Being has also played live with deZeption. Since 2019, deZeption has continued as the solo project of Jan Brink, who writes, produces and sings under the name, describing the band’s sound as “futurepop with an edge.” Brink signed deZeption to Town And Towers Records in 2024, which reissued “Human Eyes” digitally that September and released the new singles “No Sense” and “A New World Is Rising.” Side-Line has covered deZeption’s work under Town And Towers since the signing and “No Sense” release in June 2024 and the “A New World Is Rising” single in November 2024. “Am I You” continues that run and arrives as Brink works on deZeption’s third album, with the “Human Eyes” vinyl reissue marking the album’s first physical pressing since its original 2008 CDr release.

items.body: The Chameleons released their debut studio album, “Script of the Bridge,” through Statik Records on 8 August 1983. The English post-punk band from Middleton, Greater Manchester, recorded the album at Cargo Studios in Rochdale with engineer Colin Richardson. “Script of the Bridge” turns 43 this year. The classic Chameleons line-up of Mark Burgess (bass, vocals), Dave Fielding (guitar, keyboards), Reg Smithies (guitar, cover artwork) and John Lever (drums) is credited as producer alongside Richardson. Statik issued the album on vinyl LP and cassette, opening with “Don’t Fall,” which samples dialogue from the 1946 film Two Sisters from Boston, and running twelve tracks through to closer “View from a Hill.” The record includes the singles “Up the Down Escalator,” “As High as You Can Go” and “A Person Isn’t Safe Anywhere These Days.” In the United States, MCA Records issued a truncated eight-track edition under the name Chameleons U.K, omitting “Here Today,” “Less Than Human,” “Paper Tigers” and “View from a Hill.” “Script of the Bridge” streams on Spotify in its full twelve-track, remastered form. About The Chameleons The Chameleons formed in Middleton, Greater Manchester, in 1981 when bassist and vocalist Mark Burgess, guitarist Reg Smithies and guitarist Dave Fielding began playing together without a drummer; Smithies and Fielding had previously performed together as Years, while Burgess came from the Cliches. Middleton drummer Brian Schofield joined briefly before John Lever, formerly of the Politicians, took over on drums, with former Magazine drummer Martin Jackson filling in during 1982-83 while Lever was on sabbatical. After a 1981 session for BBC Radio 1 DJ John Peel, the band signed to Epic Records and released the Steve Lillywhite-produced debut single “In Shreds” in March 1982, its sleeve painted by Smithies, who created the artwork for all the band’s releases. Epic dropped the group soon after, and the Chameleons signed to Statik Records, a Virgin Records subsidiary, on which they released “Script of the Bridge” on 8 August 1983. Statik’s status as a Virgin subsidiary kept the album off the UK independent charts, but a truncated MCA Records edition built the band a college-radio following in the United States. The Chameleons followed with a second album, “What Does Anything Mean? Basically,” on Statik in 1985, then signed to Geffen Records for “Strange Times” in 1986. The death of manager Tony Fletcher in 1987 and internal tension between Burgess and Fielding led the band to split that year; Burgess and Lever went on to form the Sun and the Moon, while Smithies and Fielding formed the Reegs. The Chameleons reconvened in 2000 for shows at the Witchwood in Ashton-under-Lyne, released the acoustic album “Strip” the same year and the studio album “Why Call It Anything” in 2001, before splitting again in 2003. Burgess and Lever went on to perform the band’s catalogue as ChameleonsVox from 2009 until Lever’s death in 2017. Burgess and Smithies reformed the Chameleons under the band’s original name in 2021 with guitarist Chris Oliver and drummer Stephen Rice, both previously of ChameleonsVox, releasing the live album “Edge Sessions (Live from the Edge)” on Metropolis Records in 2022, the label the band joined that February. The reformed lineup, rounded out by keyboardist Danny Ashberry, announced a December 2022 UK tour and toured with Au Pairs singer Lesley Woods in 2023. In May 2024 the band released the “Where Are You?” EP, their first new material in over two decades, followed that October by the “Tomorrow Remember Yesterday” EP of re-recorded early tracks. The Chameleons released the single “Saviours Are A Dangerous Thing” via Metropolis Records in May 2025 ahead of their fifth studio album, “Arctic Moon,” released that September, and announced a European “Arctic Moon” tour for the fall. More than four decades after Statik released “Script of the Bridge,” the guitar-driven, atmospheric sound the album established remains the foundation the Chameleons’ later work continues to build on.

Over the years, and through line-up evolutions, this Experimental outfit has built up an impressive discography, with numerous releases appearing on a variety of labels. This latest work takes us back to 2014, when the band intended to compose a Soundtrack for a film that ultimately never came to fruition. The music, however, endured and was finally completed and released more than a decade later as a collection of eight tracks. Contrastate is known for its uncompromising Experimental sound, yet on this album it is clearly noticeable that the material was conceived as a film Soundtrack. The record is highly varied, shifting between minimalist electronic sequences and a genuine patchwork of sounds. At times, Contrastate creates an unsettling atmosphere, only to let it evolve into passages with a subtle Jazzy feel, supported by gentle rhythms. Field recordings are also present throughout the album, alongside occasional industrial elements. The album possesses a distinctly Cinematic quality, inviting the listener to imagine their own story and accompanying film. For me, this is accessible Experimental music that remains engaging without sacrificing its adventurous spirit. (Rating:7). Listen to “The Tongue Of Fire”: The Tongue Of Fire by Contrastate About Contrastate Contrastate is an experimental group formed in 1987 in London by Stephen Meixner and Jonathan Grieve, joined in 1992 by Stephen J. Pomeroy. The project grew out of earlier work under the names The Disciples of Delmonte and The State Organisation, drawing on the industrial and experimental music scene of the 1970s and 1980s as well as experimental film, theatre, and writing. Contrastate was inactive between 2000 and 2010. Releases have included “A Breeding Ground for Flies” and its 2016 vinyl/CD companion “No Eden Without Annihilation”, assembled from live recordings made across Europe between 2012 and 2014. The group’s latest album, “Seven Flies Feeding Inside The Tears Of A Woman’s Eye”, released on FinalMuzik, revisits music originally written in 2014 for an unrealized film soundtrack.

items.body: Much of Europe goes on vacation in August, so there’s no better time to release an album about “adventure, travel, and the journey of life.” The Leeds post-rock quintet Din of Celestial Birds hopes their album will be the soundtrack to many road trips, ocean voyages and international flights. The music is not only good for Takeoffs & Landings, but the time in-between. As festival season approaches, one of these trips may be to see the band in person. There’s not a second to waste as the band jumps right into it with three guitars, synth, bass and drums. The music is upbeat and punchy, adding a secret weapon: this is also post-rock that one can dance to, despite its metal overtones; a keen sense of rhythm calls fans out of the mosh pit and onto the main floor. One suspects that this aspect of the music is largely responsible for the band’s swiftly-growing reputation as a stellar live act. At 3:11, “Takeoffs & Landings” is also the rare post-rock track that qualifies as a radio single. While the music is largely aggressive, veering from post-rock to math rock to progressive rock, the moments of dynamic contrast stand out. One of these arrives early in “Marmoris” when the music calms down enough for one to hear the sounds of the shore. As the bank of guitars resurfaces and the drummer viciously attacks his drums, a sense of catharsis is palpable. The well-named “When Suddenly …” races out of the gate like the opener, then stops at 2:06; for a split-second, one thinks the track has ended, when suddenly it shifts gears to establish a base of solo piano upon which all the other instruments will build; a light choir lifts the track to the stratosphere. Two of the best tracks also contain the best post-rock titles. The first of these is “From This Summit We Can See The Heavens & Stars,” whose opening minutes are remarkably restrained, to the extent that one wonders if the track had been considered for the opening slot. The attack arrives at 2:32 in a melodic, metallic surge. This is followed by a mini-synth breakdown at 3:10, which leads to a drum roll and the summit of the title; then at 5:08, just as the track is ending, an even higher peak. Highlight “I Hope That Road Leads You Somewhere Beautiful, Somewhere You Belong” succeeds with subtlety rather than bombast; reflecting its title, the music seems slightly melancholic, a love letter to the listener. August is not only the month for vacations, but transitions, implying endings and goodbyes. This piece speaks directly to the heart, setting up the multi-toned farewell finale, “Second Star To The Right, and Straight On ‘Til Morning.” Soon the vacations will be over, the kids will be back at school, and the earth will tumble farther from the sun, but not yet; may we cherish these halcyon weeks of takeoffs and landings while we still have them. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Benga runs on interlocking guitars and a rhythm that does not let up, the sound that owned Kenyan pop for forty years. Winyo has spent twenty of those years playing it his own way, guitar in hand, singing in Luo and Swahili in a voice his countrymen named after a bird. He plays The Jago in Dalston on Sunday 9 August, a room of a couple of hundred, and most of the set is an album he has not released yet. The one piece of the record anyone can hear so far is “Mapenzi Sumu”, released in April. The title is Swahili for love is poison, and Winyo wrote it after a ten-year relationship ended. He recorded it at Ketebul Music in Nairobi, the studio behind his 2012 debut Benga Blues, with Fiston Lusambo of Afriquoi on bass, guitar and arrangement, then sent it to London for Abubilla’s Elliot Wenman to add keys, piano, synths and drums. Winyo has said he normally writes behind metaphor and this time did not, and there are lines he can barely sing without stopping. Born Shiphton Onyango on the shore of Lake Victoria, he took the Luo word for bird as his name, and twenty years of singing benga have taken him onto stages with the likes of Gilberto Gil and Vieux Farka Touré, Joss Stone and into the studio with the late Oliver Mtukudzi. The London end of that record is Abubilla Music, the label behind Winyo’s return and the promoter of this show. Kwame Otiende has run The Jago since 2018, and he grew up between Nairobi and western Kenya, the Luo country where benga started and where Winyo was born. Dalston has been dancing to benga in that room for years. items.body: A low cello refrain runs under “A Quiet Pulse” from the opening, looping and insistent, the work of Redi Hasa. The track is the second single from Sound Sketches: Music Composed for the Giorgio Armani Privé 2005–2025 Exhibition, the new album from L’Antidote, out on 18 September through Ponderosa Music Records. Hasa had the classical repertoire down by thirteen, learned in Tirana on a state-owned instrument, and he says he loves betraying that training. The 1997 civil war cut his conservatory studies short, and he reached Italy the year after on a scholarship to Lecce, carrying a cello taken from the Tirana Conservatory, the one his 2020 solo record The Stolen Cello is named for. He and his two bandmates, Iranian percussionist Bijan Chemirani and Lebanese pianist Rami Khalife, recorded “A Quiet Pulse” live off each other with nothing written down. You can hear the looseness in how the parts arrive. The cello figure keeps returning, slow and even, the piece breathing around it. Chemirani comes in on the zarb, hand and shaker work skating over the top, and Khalife’s piano arrives late, thick with reverb and echo, before a cry cuts clean through the calm. The cry runs back through both men’s histories. Chemirani learned the zarb from his father, the Persian master Djamchid Chemirani. Khalife, son of the Lebanese oud player Marcel Khalife, was born in Beirut during the civil war. L’Antidote wrote Sound Sketches for the Armani/Silos galleries in Milan, to fill the rooms as visitors move through twenty years of couture. It is their second record, though they place it at the start of everything, the point where the three of them first played as one band. The trio took their name from what Khalife says music does: an antidote to reality, something that soothes and shifts how you see things. They tour through the autumn: 22 October at Santeria Toscana 31 in Milan, 27 October at the Théâtre des Bouffes du Nord in Paris, 28 October at the Teatro Cantiere Florida in Florence for the HEARTbeat Festival, and 17 November at sPAZIO211 in Turin. items.body: Review by Chaoticreason — 3.5 stars. It would be four if they had only released 10 albums instead of 100.Okay, I am not entirely sure that anyone even gives a sh.. about this band. Are they even a band? How come they have made over 100 albums? These are all facts, according to my oracle, Google God, are true.So here is a 1st review of their music, on PA.I am not sure why I picked upon this album. The band is hugely prolific, as Ashtray Navigations, do they not even care what others make of their music? Indeed, if I had as many albums to my name as this band, I would not really care what people thought of my music. But they have nonetheless released a huge number of albums, over 100, That may or may not make them the most prolific band in history. I do not know the answer to that question, and am too scared to Google it. Just in case, it goes well beyond a mere 100 albums (I suspect it does), and is something ridiculous like 1000 albums, I simply do not want to know, the whole idea sets my mind affright.So what? You bored readers are wondering, does their music sound like?Well. I have just played their 2026 album Quad (probably one of the many albums from 2026) a few times over, and it is not the disaster zone that I had expected. Whilst it is not the best album I have heard so far this year, it is equally a very long way from being the worst. How do you sum this band up upon one single album? Well! Quite simply, you don't, you can't. How can you? So down to the music. I was astonished to hear tunes, decent enough tunes, even if nothing amazing came my way from the album. I was surprised that the music could hold my incredibly short attention span for more than a few minutes. The whole album clocks in at a merciful 44 minutes. I use the word merciful, for the simple reason that I could be spending my time listening to far better music than this (or could I?). That is in no way to say that this is bad music, it is not. I can just think of a few bands that I would rather be listening to. Yes, just a few.It is not as if this is bad music, indeed it is way more inventive than you would expect from a band with over 100 albums to their name. It is mostly that my presumption is that no band can release over 100 albums and yet still maintain any kind of momentum. Well. Ashtray Navigations has proved my theory wrong. Whilst this is not the best album I have heard this year, it is equally a really long way from being the worst.It is inventive in its deliverance and sound, It is like that interesting uncle who holds a Ph.D. in philosophy, and has a head full of great philosophical stories, that hold you rapt in attention because if you miss a single beat, you have no hope of grasping the import of that great insight. This album is way more than great background music, it is actually worth listening to. But, up alongside some of this year's better albums, it falls a bit short. But, honestly, not by all that much. It really is a rather good slab. A more than worthwhile excursion into the wonderful world of Ashtray Navigations. A great name for a band.�It still blows my mind that a band can release this many albums, and the one that I pick to listen to, really is a rather good work. Maybe I just got lucky? Who Knows? Least of all me.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 981Tangerine Dream is a progressive electronic rock band that was founded in Berlin, Germany in 1967 by Edgar Froese. Initially the band was formed as The Ones in 1965. Tangerine Dream is one of the electronic pioneers with a very extensive and amazing career. The work of them comprises several and different phases all over the years. The initial phase also called The Pink Years is the phase that is of interest for this review. As its name indicates, this is a musical phase a bit influenced by Pink Floyd. The albums that belong to that phase are the first four studio albums of Tangerine Dream, "Electronic Meditation" from 1970, "Alpha Centauri" from 1971, "Zeit" from 1972 and "Atem" from 1973.So, their initial phase began with an avant-garde and herb-rocking debut work, perhaps misleadingly titled "Electronic Meditation", because it's more a krautrock than an electronic work. In reality, it was only on their second studio album "Alpha Centauri" that the synthesizers came into play. Until then they managed to play without electronic instruments. Besides, the line up on "Electronic Meditation" isn't what is considered the classic line up of Tangerine Dream. In reality, it was only on their third studio work "Zeit" that appeared what is now considered the best line up of the band, Edgar Froese, Christopher Franke and Peter Baumann, because on their second effort "Alpha Centauri", Bauman wasn't present yet. So, "Electronic Meditation" appears to be quite a polarizing album between fans, due to that. After this album, each member went his own way, and each went on to be a renowned krautrock artist in their own way."Electronic Meditation" strongly deviates from all the other albums of the huge Tangerine Dream's catalogue. As I mentioned above, it's very ironic that "Electronic Meditation" was the only Tangerine Dream's album released in the 70's where its title didn't fit at all. It's neither electronic music made by synthesizers or meditative. The album consists apparently of experimental noises without a clear direction and purpose, performed with classic rock instruments. Nothing less representative could have been released as the debut of an electronic progressive act. In reality, this is a real rock album made with rock instruments. It's actually krautrock, the musical style invented by the German musicians in the late 60's and in the early 70's. "Electronic Meditation" is quite similar to "A Saucerful Of Secrets" and "Ummagumma" by Pink Floyd. Still, I also noticed the kind of music that Schulze later on would record with Ash Ra Tempel after he had left Tangerine Dream. Sometimes I even hear some hints of Jimi Hendrix, but also from their compatriots of Amon D��l, another krautrock German band from those days, one the best and most famous too."Electronic Meditation" has five tracks. The album starts with "Geburt (Genesis)", which is a track dominated by Schnitzler's scratchy creaking cello, combined with wild drumming and furious flute sounds performed by their guest, Keyserling. After a while something like a rhythm develops, but as soon as this is the case, the piece is already over and it goes straight and abruptly into its second track. The fittingly titled "Reise Durch Ein Brennendes Gehirn (Journey Through A Burning Brain)" begins as a freeform piece, then the organ enters with mighty tones, and finally the piece develops into a garish guitar orgy. This track encapsulates the whole krautrock vibe and it's a perfect example of crunchy rock and roll. This is probably the highlight of "Electronic Meditation". The pounding drums and acid guitar continue for "Kalter Rauch (Cold Smoke)". It begins with quiet organ sounds, which are repeatedly interrupted by short outbursts of chaos. Then the cello scrapes again, and snappy drums come and go, and another relentless psychedelic guitar attack ensues. I think it was mostly Pink Floyd that gave the inspiration to this track with its lengthy guitar/organ freak-outs. "Asche Zu Asche (Ashes To Ashes)" feels almost conventional compared to the rest of the album with a consistent rhythm and a halfway recognizable melody. The piece grows more and more furious with more distorted guitar over lazy cymbal heavy backbeat and, then suddenly, fades out. It reminds me a bit of The Doors. The concluding "Auferstehung (Resurrection)" begins with an almost solemn organ melody, to which a narrator declares a true incomprehensible text that was recorded backwards. In the further course, the theme of the opening track is taken up.Conclusion: Tangerine Dream is the best and most important electronic progressive act of the 70's and of all time, and they would over the decade make some of my all-time favourite music. Tangerine Dream is, next to Kraftwerk, the most well-known electronic formation in Germany. And just like them, they began almost entirely non-electronically. The first Tangerine Dream's album is quite a refreshing and experimentally quirky affair, quite different from the works that both Schulze and Froese later released. The five tracks are certainly worth listening to. I think the music here is probably better digested for many people than some of the material on their earlier real electronic albums. Besides, "Electronic Meditation" is a nice way to discover how Tangerine Dream started their career. And, all in all, the music on this album is probably a pleasant and interesting surprise, especially for those who are huge fans of the krautrock style of music.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by Abrasmatheus — Coming to this album, I expected something much closer to the band's later soft rock sound. Like many listeners, I first knew Ambrosia through songs such as "Biggest Part of Me," so discovering their self-titled debut was quite a surprise. Rather than polished adult contemporary, this record presents a fascinating blend of melodic soft rock and progressive rock, creating an identity that feels both sophisticated and accessible. It easily exceeded my expectations.One of the album's greatest strengths is the balance between memorable melodies and progressive arrangements. While the music rarely reaches the complexity of the major symphonic prog bands of the era, it incorporates shifting structures, rich keyboard textures, dynamic contrasts, and tasteful instrumental passages without sacrificing accessibility. The result is an album that can appeal both to progressive rock fans and to listeners who enjoy melodic rock from the 1970s.The opening track, "Nice, Nice, Very Nice," immediately establishes this identity. Its polished production, layered vocals, and elegant keyboard work remind me at times of the atmosphere later associated with The Alan Parsons Project, while still maintaining Ambrosia's own personality. It is an excellent introduction and one of the reasons the album makes such a strong first impression.My favorite tracks are "Time Waits for No One," "Holdin' on to Yesterday," and especially "Make Us All Aware." The latter stands out for its stronger progressive character, interesting rhythmic development, and satisfying structural variations. Another highlight is "Mama Frog," whose instrumental approach occasionally brings to mind the energy of Emerson, Lake & Palmer and even some of King Crimson's more adventurous moments. The closing epic, "Drink of Water," is another outstanding composition, giving me the feeling of hearing Crosby, Stills & Nash interpreted through a progressive rock lens. It is a beautiful and memorable conclusion to the album.Instrumentally, the album is consistently enjoyable. The keyboards and synthesizers play a central role, adding color and atmosphere throughout the record, while the vocals remain expressive without becoming overdramatic. The musicianship is polished, serving the songs rather than existing simply to demonstrate technical ability.Although the album incorporates obvious soft rock influences, I still consider it a genuinely progressive rock release. The frequent changes in mood, carefully crafted arrangements, extended compositions, and willingness to experiment separate it from conventional soft rock albums of the period. At the same time, it avoids excessive complexity, jazz-oriented improvisation, or the grand symphonic approach that characterized many of its contemporaries. That accessibility is one of its greatest strengths rather than a weakness.Lyrically, I did not focus closely on the individual songs, but they complement the reflective and uplifting atmosphere created by the music. Combined with the warm production and melodic songwriting, the album maintains a consistently pleasant listening experience from beginning to end.Perhaps the greatest compliment I can give this album is that I never find myself wanting to skip a track. There are no weak moments here, and each song contributes something meaningful to the overall flow. The atmosphere is inviting, melodic, and subtly adventurous, making it an album I continue returning to years after first discovering it.I would recommend this record to anyone who enjoys the intersection of progressive rock and 1970s soft rock. Listeners who demand highly technical, symphonic, or heavy progressive music may find it too restrained, but those looking for sophisticated songwriting with progressive touches should find plenty to appreciate.

items.body: Review by Aussie-Byrd-Brother — Nearly sixty years into their existence, legendary rock band Yes may never recapture that dynamic, extravagant and inspired edge that made them one of the defining prog-rock bands of the Seventies, but that doesn't mean there's nothing left of worth with the current line-up and their recent releases. Mostly driven by longtime guitarist Steve Howe, here aided by frequent contributors - keyboardist Geoff Downes, bass player Billy Sherwood, former Glass Hammer frontman Jon Davison and more recent drummer Jan Schellen - this incarnation of the symphonic institution (having navigated the loss of founding bassist Chris Squire and longtime drummer Alan White) returns with their fourth album together, and twenty-sixth studio work overall, 2026's `Aurora', that shows them still offering colourful, adventurous and melodic rock that many die-hard fans will enjoy.Title track `Aurora' is a glorious and slick opener, where fancy orchestration, calling to mind their 2001 Album `Magnification', swoons around Steve Howe's reaching guitar strains, Billy Sherwood honouring the tradition of the late Chris Squire's upfront bass rumbles and a flighty Jon Davison vocal. Joyful with rousing reprises of striking themes, it makes for a memorable and impressive opener about evoking transformation and connection, and damned if "Like paper doves in a cut-out world..." ain't a darn adorable lyric!Despite lovely group harmonies and little pockets of fancy instrumental touches, `Turnaround Situation' doesn't hold together particularly well as a whole, but there's lovely buoyant bass and fancy acoustic flourishes racing alongside each-other throughout the dreamy and romantic (and better) `Love Lies Dreaming', perhaps vocally and musically one of the prettiest pieces of the disc.Being the longest track on the album at near fourteen minutes will instantly pique the interest of most prog-rock fans, but...lower that eyebrow, mister! Sadly the four-part `Countermovement', contemplating human authenticity, comes across as more a collection of fragments and half-completed passages rather than a coherent and flowing whole, but there are a nice range of tempo-shifts back and forth, and a lot of focus put on both Steve Howe's humble and pensive vocal and a range of versatile guitar solo spots.With `Ariadne', Yes adopts a storytelling approach of so many prog bands old and new, looking to myth and legend for inspiration, and it suitably surges forwards with Jan's strident drumming and delicate orchestration that soars with classical fancy. At its heart it recounts the mythological Greek tale of Princess Ariadne and the Minotaur's labyrinth, which the band also uses it as a metaphor for being lost, with lines like "With walls around you, you're trapped in your own space", and finally taking control. Howe's guitar adds a heroic flavour and urgency, and it's nice to hear group harmonies from several members together throughout.Despite a fairly banal lyric about springing to action, `All Hands on Deck' is quite fun with jaunty keyboard/guitar interplay, made memorable by Steve's guitar grunt that takes on a bluesier toughness in little bursts, and it's nice to hear Jon singing a little more naturally deeper throughout too! In what could probably be considered an interlude, the three minute `Outside the Box' is primarily an instrumental. Framed by a constantly morphing set of wordless sighing group harmonies, they're interspersed with an eclectic grab-bag of fuzzy electronic swirls, jamming bass/guitar duels and intricate drum patterns across a range of tempos back and forth.Short and sweet, soft-rocker `Emotional Intelligence' opens with gentle piano, unassuming acoustic strums and the warm hum of Hammond organ, Davison softly offering a call to understanding and unity with its well-meaning lyric. It briefly springs up to life near its climax with slide guitar wisps, and this compact little album closer displays restraint and tastefulness throughout.All versions of `Aurora' come with two pieces that are classed as bonus tracks, but they are actually both worthwhile inclusions that don't disrupt the flow of the core album or come across as mere throwaways. `Jambustin' (really just a fun way to refer to being `cut off'), is a warning against negative behaviours and arguing with or obstructing others, displaying a jauntiness in its verses and a softly grooving chorus with slinking bass. Despite a fairly overused motive of moving water as a metaphor for life and the passing of time, `Watching the River Roll' embraces the theme with acceptance and peace, and it delivers dreamy and shimmering instrumentation (not to mention constantly drifting Moog solos!) and bristles with an upbeat, life-affirming positivity that glides with energy.Yes has always had more to offer than just the contributions of former vocalist Jon Anderson and keyboardist Rick Wakeman, and modern, worthwhile work from both of those artists can easily be found elsewhere, so their absence doesn't take anything away from this current version of the group. Some pockets of the fanbase will find their exclusion absolutely inexcusable, meaning there's no coming back from that, but Yes has constantly had an eclectic revolving door of imaginative, skilled and varied musicians that have all made exciting contributions to the overall Yes sound throughout the decades.Despite being a little overlong and delivering a couple of less successful pieces, Yes have delivered an enjoyable disc of vibrant and eclectic rock in `Aurora', always melodic without falling into overtly poppy or radio-friendly banality and full of interesting instrumental details. Given several re-spins, it proves to be valid addition to the Yes legacy, with the current incarnation looking to their past but still moving forward in interesting and rewarding ways, and if you appreciate the wider world of Yes music from a range of musicians, chances are you'll find much to enjoy here.Three and a half stars.

items.body: Review by Chaoticreason — 4.5 stars. I have a strange relationship with this band (then again, that is true of every band that I listen to). I generally put all my albums (some 2,500 or so, many more sit in the sidelines waiting for me to pick them up again, post removal from my playlist) on random play, so I frequently forget who the band is that I am playing. It ends up being a game of Russian roulette (no pun intended). Like hearing an album for the 1st time, except that you know the music, but can't remember the artist. I must confess to being blown away sometimes by a Roz Vitalis album that comes up randomly, and at other times thinking what the heck is this Rubbish. This is all of course down to how receptive my head is at that moment in time. All good music has its place in my playlist, but my head is not always up for some of the completely wild atonal stuff that is on my playlist. Whilst Roz Vitalis are certainly not in that category, of being for very specific moments, they have enough of an edge to sometimes make me love them and other times not want to play them. Whilst this may sound bad for my love of this band, that is quite simply not the case. Sometimes I love the Beatles, or some early Bob, but not all the time.So what do I make of this 25th anniversary record? Well, as it uses some of the highlight tracks from their vast opus, there are tracks on here that I do already know, but some of the arrangements have me guessing. I would say the band have played it fairly safe for long-term fans, it is a great idea to mix some old material with new sounds. I would also say, for sure, that this is a great introduction to a band that can push its sonic boundaries well beyond anything that they have done here. This is not to denigrate this record, I just feel that they wished to capture the more listenable side of their music, as opposed to alienating everybody with a full on expose of just how weird and wonderful their sound can be at times.Violinist, Vitaly Borodin certainly deserves mention, I only know his work with Vespero (another great Russian band), but will happily seek out the other bands he has played in (they being The Legendary Flower Punk & Vevil). He, as the rest of the band do, appear to have all had an obvious classically trained background. Still, the man sticks some really great solo work into this recording, that bares no real resemblance to what I think of as Classically trained violinist as doing. He plays an almost gypsy style (which I love) that overrides his classical training.So to sum this album up!Well, I would say that it is definitely a great gateway into their music, for those who have perhaps been put off in the past by their more oblique albums, (personally I love the more out there stuff. But! Only if I am in the mood). It is also great to hear some old tunes rearranged, especially with Vitaly Borodin on board, the band have really let him do his thing, as only he can do.This is definitely an album worth listening to if you have the slightest interest in music that pushes boundaries, but does not smash them to pieces, at least not here. (Totally free on Bandcamp as of writing this). This is a great place to start for such a diverse and original band. Not too much weirdness, but just enough for those sat on the fence to go for it. The recording quality makes it sound, at least, to my ears, as if it was recorded in a studio. Others may have a very different take on that thought, it is just my opinion.A great 25th anniversary recording.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The Norwegian duo of H�kon Oftung and Kristian Fr�land continues to craft increasingly rich and subtle works. Following an introduction titled "Invokasjon", which could well serve as a compendium of the entire repertoire to follow, "Sankeren" kicks off with a sharp, aggressive electric guitar attack; yet, as H�kon Oftung begins to sing, those strange harmonies, so characteristic of Wigwam and practically patented by the Finnish band in the 70s, hovering somewhere between sacred music and atonal contemporary classical, start to emerge amidst the Minimoogs and Mellotrons. Then comes a section featuring a clavinet and a rhythm bordering on heavy metal, albeit in a symphonic vein, with arpeggios reminiscent of Mike Oldfield's Tubular Bells. The balance between instrumental and vocal passages is remarkable; after such high-speed intensity, an almost jazzy calm sets in, intimate and steeped in nocturnal darkness. Having steadily evolved their compositional style since 2017's Jord, by the time Salighet arrived, Jordsj� had truly come into their own."Salighet I", with its blend of acoustic guitar, flute, and clavinet, possesses the modern feel characteristic of the later Gryphon era; yet the album's defining feature is the work of the two musicians, a duo with such deep familiarity and seamless sonic and instrumental interplay that they take the Wigwam formula a step further. They are worthy successors, as their acoustic guitar and flute excursions brush against acoustic psychedelia before shifting abruptly into a new section, such is the richness of the album's musical vision. Bass clarinets and oboes also make themselves heard, creating an unusual atmosphere that reminded me of Marty Ehrlich's 1999 album Sojourn.In "Salighet II," on the other hand, the electric guitar and keyboard seem to tell a story; there is something mystical, an aura of discovery, as well as suspense, yet whether the music is in a slow or fast section, the momentum never flags, nor does the listener's attention. The flute enters at just the right moment, as does the clavinet.By the time the fifth track, "Ura," arrives, the mood is fully set; the polished precision reminiscent of Tubular Bells blends with the mysterious guitar notes in the vein of Jukka Tolonen. Towards the end, the guitar strums in isolation against a swelling keyboard, the air grows heavy and dense, while the Minimoog improvises, hovering between progressive rock and jazz-rock. Medieval darkness gives way to a frenetic, syncopated rhythm that stumbles and rises, stumbles and rises, gradually finding its own groove. In "Danseritualer fra Jordsj� - Prosesjon & Ekstase," the pastoral flute appears like a rainbow, only to be obscured by a free-form psychedelic interplay of bass and electric guitar."Stjernestigen" takes a dramatic turn, evoking a classical-leaning Chick Corea, yet there is something truly special about that oboe, the acoustic guitar, which later shifts to electric, and the impeccable vocals. The music unfolds with a Minimoog reminiscent at times of Wakeman and a jazzy piano flowing like a fresh breeze, all wrapped in an eternal mystery, one they will not reveal, for perhaps it is better that way; having learned the lesson of the past, they understand that the continuation of an unfinished ending holds the greatest promise of eternity.
