items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — References to Emerson, Lake & Palmer are unavoidable in "The Seven Movements of the Third Majesty", the first of three tracks making up the second album by Ring Van M�bius (themselves a trio). Yet, starting with "The 3rd Majesty," they truly make the 70s sound their own, playing with such feeling, emotion, and conviction that they earn the right to wear their influences openly. After all, there is a fine line between merely copying a sound for convenience and channeling an influence born of years of listening and a genuine love for the genre, a path to finding one's own voice that even the greatest bands have walked, and one that ultimately comes down to the individual listener's taste. The surging Minimoog lines, the frenetic, air-slicing drums, and the bass advancing like a blitzkrieg leave no doubt; shifting from rock-style Hammond organ to jazzier tones, the only thing left to do is enjoy the superb musicianship and the fresh melodies, melodies that resemble constellations in the cosmos. Just as the scientific community discovers new ones, isn't that the perfect terrain for progressive rock? Space constellations... suddenly, the tempo slows, leaving the bass, drums, and Thor Erik Helgesen's vocals floating as if in a sci-fi series.Around the midpoint of the track, the organ takes on a distorted sound, accompanied by bass and drums that turn psychedelic, and at times they abandon their polished approach for a raw sound, losing the melody and improvising; the same applies to the vocalist, who lets loose and screams, not like Hammill, but in his own style, lending the music a vibrant, original character.Things get heavy towards the end of "The Seven Movements of the Third Majesty"; the organ takes on an atonal, distorted sound, reminiscent of Van der Graaf Generator, marking the moment Ring Van M�bius truly comes into its own as a trio. It is not just about their playing, but also their composition and passionate execution, the third pillar of a great band on a great album."Illuminati" may continue to evoke Tarkus in their instrumental work, but Thor Erik Helgesen's vocal style leans closer to Deep Purple, yielding a completely different result; then they shift into jazz-rock, and a Renaissance-style section takes over, followed by instrumental passages featuring electric clavichord underpinned by drums and bass, the likes of which one might think we would no longer hear these days. Yet, the raw Norwegian intensity of the performance makes it feel new, original, and fresh. When the vocals need to be high-pitched and delicate, they deliver just that, and in the span of a mere five minutes, "Illuminati" manages to encompass the feel of multiple different songs."Distant Sphere" features a string section, and the shift in texture works beautifully; the arrangement is highly original, as is the way the trio enters immediately after, creating a space-like atmosphere with bass and Rhodes keyboard. When the drums kick in, it sounds like a trio featuring Bill Bruford, John Wetton, and Dave Stewart. The composition here is far more experimental, it is hard to believe it is just a trio, with the keyboard once again distorted to the point of frenzy; meanwhile, when they play jazz, they do so with an admirable groove, proving themselves worthy heirs to the Norwegian tradition in this regard as well. They also infuse the music with an ethereal, mysterious quality characteristic of space rock, a genre that influenced 1970s jazz-rock, and now influences them."The M�bius Ring" is a Yes-style rock track featuring Chris Squire-esque bass work; yet, when Thor Erik Helgesen sings, he makes the song his own, imbuing it with the band's signature stamp, a noble wildness reminiscent of fur coats and boots. The keyboards provide a grand, symphonic finale that gives way to the bass, where H�vard Rasmussen proves himself every bit as virtuosic as his bandmates. On drums, Dag Olav Hus�s even plays the timpani to mirror Thor Erik Helgesen's vocal inflections. It is a majestic journey, driven by a Minimoog line that stretches toward the horizon, where the sky meets a sea teeming with monsters promising unforgettable adventures, before looping back in a circular path: like a M�bius strip, like a ring, and like the trio's discography, which was just beginning here.

items.body: Feel it now and don’t resistThis time the anger’s better than the kissI must admit when so inclinedI tend to lose it than confront my mind Some songs that become so closely associated with their original performers that covering them feels a little like borrowing somebody else’s leather jacket. You might fit into it, you might even look terrific, but everybody remembers who wore it first. The Afghan Whigs’ Debonair is one of those numbers, loaded with Greg Dulli’s particular combination of seduction, self-disgust, and barely concealed bad intentions. Seattle’s Ghosts in the Graveyard approach it with enough confidence to make the jacket theirs. There is also something pleasantly strange about hearing an Afghan Whigs song pulled toward deathrock. The original already had danger baked into its bones, so the transformation feels less like genre tourism than discovering that two people from different neighborhoods have been drinking at the same questionable bar for years. The band gives Debonair a harder goth-rock frame, pushing the guitars forward while electronic accents gather around the edges. Byron C. Miller sings with the dramatic authority the material requires, leaning into the song’s appetite for trouble without treating Dulli’s original performance as sacred text. Paul Morgan’s guitar work supplies much of the momentum, moving between muscular chords and sharper details while the arrangement maintains the nightclub immediacy that has become central to Ghosts in the Graveyard. That relationship becomes clearer in the accompanying video, directed and edited by Miller and shot by cinematographer Ryan Purcell. The band performs inside a small club surrounded by an enthusiastic audience, with the camera catching bodies pressed toward the stage and musicians feeding off the room. Rather than turning the performance into an elaborate visual concept, the clip concentrates on physical proximity and the chemistry between band and crowd. It gives Debonair the slightly dangerous communal charge that rock music tends to acquire when there are fewer than six feet between the singer and somebody holding a beer. Watch the video for Debonair below: The cover will close Ghosts in the Graveyard’s forthcoming Monsters for the Masses: Resurrected, due this October through Re:Mission Entertainment. The record revisits the band’s 2016 album for its tenth anniversary, rebuilding the material from the ground up following the expanded reach of 2025’s Absolute Death. With Miller joined by Morgan, keyboardist Kaylie Cortez, and vocalist Shelly Smith, the current lineup has developed into a formidable live unit, something the Debonair video makes immediately apparent. Choosing this song as the album’s final word makes sense. Debonair has always sounded like somebody smiling while making several decisions they will regret tomorrow morning. Ghosts in the Graveyard preserve the song’s wicked little grin, then surround it with bigger guitars, gothic drama, and the welcome possibility that someone in the front row may lose a shoe. items.body: Somewhere along the line, coldwave became frighteningly good at keeping its shirt tucked in. The drum machines behave, the bass sits precisely where expected, everyone owns an appropriate black coat, and occasionally you begin wondering whether an entire subculture has been sentenced to spend eternity posing beside the same concrete wall. Then along comes Mercury Girl with Low Altitude, sounding sufficiently nervous to remind you that this music once existed because somebody had something eating at them. Mercury Girl is the project of Filipino American San Diego musician Aaron Pena, whose debut album, A NuTone, arrives October 10. Low Altitude is its first single, and anxiety is practically another instrument in the arrangement. The drum machine keeps clipping forward at odd little angles while synth lines twitch overhead, creating the sensation of machinery functioning perfectly while its operator quietly considers pulling the emergency brake. Then there is that bassline, lofty and strangely buoyant beneath Pena’s dissonant vocal, which seems emotionally several rooms removed from the comparatively hopeful chords surrounding it. A guitar eventually climbs through the arrangement with considerably more grandeur, briefly opening the ceiling before everything settles again into the song’s peculiar state of suspended agitation. Black Marble, Harsh Symmetry, Molchat Doma, and Oppenheimer Analysis provide obvious relational coordinates, yet Pena understands the essential reason those records work: electronics can be emotionally merciless precisely because machines have no obligation to console anybody. Put a vulnerable voice beside a rigid drum pattern and suddenly every beat sounds like another second you have survived. “This song reflects on a breakthrough I had when coming to terms with my depression,” says Pena. “I wanted to write a song capturing the internal isolation I’ve felt within me for a long time while echoing the catharsis I had after fully acknowledging it.” Which could have produced a painfully earnest five-minute therapy session set to synthesizers, an occupational hazard of anybody writing openly about their own head. Pena has enough musical sense to leave the feelings inside the machinery, where they become stranger and more useful. Low Altitude carries its emotional trouble through repetition, distance, and those unexpectedly optimistic chords, suggesting the peculiar moment when understanding yourself provides relief without magically solving anything. Listen to Low Altitude below and order the single here. Low Altitude by Mercury Girl Recorded at home in San Diego, A NuTone will expand upon Pena’s experiences with depression, isolation, love, and the difficult business of accepting affection when your own brain occasionally argues against the proposition. Low Altitude makes an excellent introduction because beneath all those cold machines sits an old rock-and-roll problem with a very human soul, trying to figure out how to live inside himself. items.body: Chasing patterns Warnings and the like Recognizing signs You can see them too Some records are best understood by the room they create around you. Hermaphrodite, the new album from Phoenix industrial artist YZBL, turns that room into a place where the walls feel close, the floor seems unstable, and every beat lands with the private force of a thought you would rather keep buried. YZBL, pronounced “Jezebel,” has carried some of this physicality since her time in industrial goth trio Tassel, yet the music here feels newly concentrated, as though every spare element has been pulled toward one central question: who gets to decide what a body means? The album’s third single, “Patterns,” brings dub and trip-hop deeper into YZBL’s industrial vocabulary. The beat moves with a narcotic drag, leaving enough empty space for the low end to feel enormous, while the heavier passages suggest Godflesh filtered through the nocturnal unease of Tricky. There is also a funereal beauty in the surrounding textures that brings This Mortal Coil to mind, especially in the way density and delicacy can occupy the same few seconds without smoothing each other out. Where others might find only pain in dysphoria, YZBL finds a kind of power. Androgyny and hermaphroditism are words the artist reclaims deliberately. Her interest is not in a body that is read by others, but about a life built apart from those readings entirely Across Hermaphrodite, dysphoria runs alongside a hard-won sense of power. YZBL treats androgyny and hermaphroditism as reclaimed language, terms used to clear space away from the gaze of people eager to classify the body. Her writing approaches identity with the bodily directness of Kathy Acker: intimate, confrontational, occasionally ugly by design, and alert to the violence hidden inside ordinary categories. The record’s minimal rhythms give those ideas room to breathe, while drones and thick guitar weight make the questions feel physical rather than academic. The album’s core ultimately challenges the binary, not only externally imposed but also internalized by the artist. “I am most transphobic towards myself,” they controversially say, describing a lifelong war fought against the idea that “difference” is wrong. That physical unease reaches its sharpest visual form in the black-and-white video for Patterns,” made by YZBL and Ash Barrett. The camera finds her in a dark, abandoned, dungeon-like space, lit by a single bulb as she scratches marks into the surface around her. The imagery carries the raw panic of The Blair Witch Project, but its performance-art severity belongs to YZBL’s own world: part confinement, part self-documentation, part evidence left behind. Watch the video for Patterns below: Hermaphrodite‘s force comes from the solidarity underneath all that weight. YZBL writes from a place where no assigned category, chosen identity, or outside reading can fully contain a person. By turning that uncertainty into rhythm, pressure, and language, she makes ambiguity feel less like a void than a territory worth defending. Existing on your own terms becomes a form of possession: of the body, of the room, and finally of the name you choose to answer to. Out now through Lana Del Rabies’ Feral Crone Recordings, the album makes its title part of the argument. The word is intentionally loaded, reclaimed, and held up as a declaration of life beyond somebody else’s categories. items.body: It comes back to control me What it said is stuck on me It comes from the shadows So elusive to me Portland duo Princess Ugly approach labour as something closer to possession on their new single, The Work, turning the ordinary language of obligation into a study of creation, anxiety, and control. J. Christopher-Rome’s lyrics begin with familiar pressures: unfinished tasks, the reluctance to ask for help, the nagging sense that something remains unresolved…before those pressures acquire a strange agency of their own. Work ceases to feel like an activity and begins behaving like a presence, capable of following its creator home. Christopher Moncrieffe builds that unease into the arrangement through clipped electronic rhythms, stern bass movement, and the mechanical forward motion of classic EBM. There is enough post-punk space around the instrumentation for Rome’s voice to carry the psychological weight, while the programming maintains a physical momentum suited equally to headphones and a crowded club. The tension comes from how naturally those two impulses coexist: the body is encouraged to move while the mind gets trapped inside a recurring thought. Rome delivers the words with the exhausted concentration of someone attempting to identify a fear while still living inside it. Memory becomes another form of labour, something requiring constant maintenance before it can be trusted, and even dreams appear subordinate to productivity. Images of dust, unfinished construction, and something sharp waiting in the dark give the song an almost metaphysical dimension. Creation rises out of debris, yet the resulting object seems capable of turning upon its maker. The song recognizes a contemporary condition in which occupation, identity, output, and self-worth have become increasingly difficult to separate. You build something, maintain it, remember why you started, and eventually discover that the structure has developed requirements of its own. Princess Ugly allows that cycle to remain unresolved, which suits a piece concerned with repetition and the unease of never reaching completion. Watch the video for The Work below: Listen to the Leæther Strip Remix of The Work below and order the single here. The Work (Leæther Strip Remix) by Princess Ugly Claus Larsen pushes those instincts toward the dance floor on the accompanying LEÆTHER STRIP Remix. His version thickens the percussion and sharpens the electro-industrial attack, giving the track a harder, more immediate propulsion without losing its underlying dread. Larsen treats the original’s anxiety as fuel, transforming psychological pressure into movement. Together, the two versions make The Work feel less like a conventional song about employment than an examination of creation becoming obligation, obligation becoming authority, and authority eventually learning how to follow you home. items.body: “Cold fear making you feel inside” is an odd line to dance to, which is precisely why it suits Scary Nights, the new single from Dream Council, the Berlin-based project of Sean Michael Pheanis. The song belongs to that useful strain of synth-pop in which pleasure and unease share the same room, each sharpening the other. Its hook is immediate, its beat clipped and insistent, and its synths carry the lacquered cool of an 80s television performance viewed at midnight with the volume turned higher than wisdom recommends. Pheanis has been moving toward this music for years. Raised in the Chicago suburbs, he began in DIY punk, putting out friends’ recordings through a homemade label before a MicroKORG and the records of Adult., The Faint, and Fischerspooner redirected his attention. Bachelor Party Weekend followed, mixing dance-punk with an eccentric new-wave bounce, after which New York and the early Bushwick witch-house scene supplied another vocabulary. Later came Los Angeles, where the city’s darkwave community helped Dream Council settle into a clearer identity, and then Berlin, where Pheanis completed the project’s self-titled debut LP. That history can be heard in Scary Nights, though the song carries its references lightly. There is something of The Human League, LCD Soundsystem, and even a little Thompson Twins in its vocals and catchy melodics, while the sterner club architecture recalls modern contemporaries Buzz Kull, Kontravoid, and Blone Noble. Synth-pop works best when the machinery serves a memorable tune. The chorus has the tidy inevitability of a phrase one seems to know before hearing it, and the arrangement keeps finding small ways to increase the pressure around it. This song is catchy as hell. The accompanying video extends that sense of private unease. Pheanis appears alone in a club after closing time, moving in slow motion through a space built for crowds, flirtation, and communal release. With nobody left to watch, the dance becomes stranger and more personal. Empty floors and dormant lights turn the nightclub into a temporary kingdom for one, a place where fear can be indulged, stylized, and perhaps exhausted before morning. The conceit also gives the song a sly visual joke: dance music has finally secured the dance floor it always wanted, only to discover that absolute freedom can look suspiciously close to isolation. Watch the video for Scary Nights below: There is an appealing continuity between the song and Pheanis’s long sequence of relocations. Chicago, New York, Los Angeles, and Berlin each contributed something to Dream Council, and “Scary Nights” gathers those years into a remarkably assured piece of pop writing. Mixed by California engineer Frank Royal and due on the forthcoming self-titled album through Lollipop Records, it suggests an artist who has finally found the right room for all the music he has been carrying around. items.body: So many things to learn, so many to unlearn To be in company and to be alone So many things I thought I cannot live without Now are disappearing, now are dissolving like clouds Boris Kaplunovich has spent much of his life moving between places that might reasonably be called home. Born in Belarus, raised in Israel, and now based in Berlin, the musician from Totenwald and Day Clinic approaches his new solo project with the accumulated perspective of someone accustomed to departures, reinvention, and the strange persistence of attachment. Tall Grass, his latest single, turns those experiences toward something intimate: the possibility that certain people find one another despite geography, history, and timing conspiring against them. Released July 25th as the first single from an EP expected this autumn, Tall Grass began with Kaplunovich lying in an unruly patch of grass in the middle of a city park. The setting provides central tension: a pocket of accidental wilderness surrounded by streets, buildings, appointments, and all the machinery by which urban life keeps time. Kaplunovich considers love from a similar position, contemplating encounters that seem improbable until, in retrospect, they acquire the peculiar logic of inevitability. The lyrics move between learning and unlearning, solitude and companionship, loss and recurrence. Possessions and old certainties dissolve, while affection survives through smaller gestures: sharing rain, lying together in tall grass, accepting mistakes that may return. At its center sits the consoling thought that two lives might repeatedly find each other, regardless of when history happened to place them on the earth. An acoustic guitar establishes the song’s modest frame before the arrangement gradually opens around it. Electronic tones enter with care, and the post-punk influence comes through in the use of space, repetition, and an occasional chill in the instrumentation. Kaplunovich sings with the plainspoken intimacy of a musician who understands how much weight understatement can carry. His phrasing leaves room around individual words, giving the performance the feeling of thoughts still taking shape as they are spoken. Gratitude runs through Tall Grass, complicated by an awareness that permanence is largely wishful thinking. People meet, circumstances change, cities absorb their inhabitants, and affection becomes inseparable from the knowledge that every shared moment belongs to a finite sequence. Kaplunovich finds tenderness within that recognition without turning it into easy consolation. Robert Hanna’s black-and-white video places Kaplunovich among neglected corners of the city: empty lots, worn concrete, industrial remnants, and abandoned spaces whose original purposes have become difficult to determine. He carries his guitar through these locations as a solitary troubadour, while Hanna finds striking geometry in broken walls, open ground, and severe urban surfaces. The photography gives Kaplunovich’s isolation a cinematic scale while preserving the song’s close, personal character. Watch the video for Tall Grass below: Following last October’s debut single, Be Them All, and years spent sharing stages with artists including Micah P. Hinson and Matt Elliott, Tall Grass brings Kaplunovich’s solo direction into sharper focus. His subject is belonging, understood here as a temporary alignment of people, place, and time. For a few minutes, lying together in the grass is enough. Listen to Tall Grass below and order the single here. items.body: Spike Hellis Successor Over-Pop Spike Hellis’ self-titled 2022 debut LP was wild, unpredictable and unexpected. Part of what made the Los Angeles duo’s take on gnarly mutant body music feel so nervy and dangerous was its aggressive switch-ups, slamming from funky EBM into anxious synthscapes and moody sample cut-ups, all anchored by Lainey Chang and Cortland Gibson’s rancorous vocals. Paired with their furious live shows, which featured the duo crawling over a jungle gym of equipment while a neon sign invited you to dial 1-888-FKN-WEAK, it made Spike Hellis impossible to ignore. Chang and Gibson’s new LP Successor takes all the spite, all the sweat, and all the smart programming and arrangement that made them so compelling, and boils it down to an even more potent and addictive formulation. It manages the trick of being both very minimal and absolutely enormous; at any given moment there could be little more than a bassline, a sample and a smattering percussion sounds going on, but each of those disparate elements is tuned and positioned for maximum impact. Debut single “By God” places a funky cowbell and crushed synth stabs on top of its burbling synth bass for one of the most addictive grooves of the year, and that’s before the shouted and sung vocals lob the song into brand new territory. Simultaneously, the Art-of-Noise-through-a-mirror-darkly “Entirely Mine” folds its repeated vocal samples into new shapes, ardent and punchy, but also steady and focused. The sheer power of the record lies in its meticulous arrangement, how everything is placed in the mix, and the space left between each drum hit, shout, sample, or synth note. “Your Successor” doesn’t sound complicated, but there’s a wealth of variation in how Chang’s half-rapped vocals bounce off the off-kilter drum programming, the stereo spread of the slow moving background textures and the tiny ripples of digital artifacting that flow into the outro. It’s none of it accidental, whether at their most noisy (“Pareplaneta”, which explodes and then lets you sit uncomfortably in the echoes) or their most accessible (the surprisingly touching “Pillow Talk”, whose bright chirps and barks manage to sound melancholic) every element is purposeful, and adds to the strength of the whole. And that’s all before we get into how ferocious and ornery Chang and Gibson are on the mic. And what’s more, that ire is cutting, and as refined and strategic as any other aspect of the album. There’s a genuine meanness to the sing-songy chorus of “Temptation” (“Feels like every time we turn around/these two petty fuckers run their mouths”) that suggests that whoever Hellis are addressing knows they’re being called out and would do well to duck them going forward. It’s a sort of calm antipathy that can be righteous (“Enemy Lines”), menacing (“Unwound (Get Right)”), or disdainful (“No Bite”), but is never obnoxious, no matter how spicy or bitter it might come across. Successor is Spike Hellis distilled; all the raw energy, all the movement, all the combativeness of their debut is here, but made sleeker, and delivered in more calculated fashion. And bizarrely, it ends up being both bracingly intense, and a whole lot of fun to listen to. It shouldn’t be possible to sound this unbothered and cool and this savage at the same time, but here we are; Spike Hellis are working hard, but you’ll never see them sweat. Highly recommended. Mari Kattman, joining all headline dates as special guest, is known for her solo work as well as her role in Helix, her ongoing collaboration with Tom Shear, and mastering work for numerous artists across the industrial, EBM and synthpop scenes. The 2007 album “Meta” produced the single “Binary,” which reached the Top 25 of the Billboard U.S. singles chart, and was followed by “Compass” in 2009, “Bruise” in 2012, “Endure” in 2016 and “Mourn” in 2020. Assemblage 23 released its tenth studio album, “Null,” via Metropolis Records on 7 November 2025, preceded by the singles “Tolerate” and “Believe.” The October 2026 European tour, with Kattman as support on every date, brings “Null” to club audiences in Germany and Sweden following the band’s summer festival run.

items.body: Belgian electro-industrial act Suicide Commando releases “Destroyer of Worlds (SGNLS Version)” via Out Of Line Music on 7 August 2026. The track is a collaboration with dark techno and EBM project DSTRTD SGNL, who rework the industrial architecture Johan Van Roy built for the original. Destroyer of Worlds (SGNLS Version) by Suicide Commando “Destroyer of Worlds” first appeared on Suicide Commando’s most recent studio album, “Goddestruktor,” released in 2022, which reached number 9 on the official German album charts. For the SGNLS Version, DSTRTD SGNL apply their dark techno and EBM production approach to the track, reshaping its structure for club and festival play while keeping Van Roy’s original vocal and industrial framework intact. DSTRTD SGNL is the German duo of Stephan Kessler and Torben Schmidt, active since 2021 in techno, EBM and dark electro, with a catalog of singles, EPs and remixes released mainly through Infacted Recordings, including collaborative work with acts such as Ruined Conflict and Mängelexemplar. The release arrives as Suicide Commando marks 40 years of activity, having formed in 1986. The project’s recent anniversary release, “Collective Suicide Vol. 1+2,” gathers material spanning early demo tapes through reworked classics alongside the new track “Control & Consent.” It is available on limited colored vinyl and as a strictly limited Wooden Fan Box Set restricted to 200 copies, containing a Digipak CD, colored double vinyl editions of both volumes and a 36-page photo book covering the band’s history. Suicide Commando live dates Suicide Commando has confirmed the following live dates: 22.08.2026 – Sao Paulo, Brazil 29.08.2026 – Mexico City, Mexico 11.12.2026 – Bielefeld, Germany 12.12.2026 – Oberhausen, Germany 15.01.2027 – Barcelona, Spain 16.01.2027 – Madrid, Spain About Suicide Commando Suicide Commando is the solo project of Belgian musician and producer Johan Van Roy, who began experimenting with electronic music in 1986. He self-released demo tapes through the late 1980s before being signed by the German label Off Beat, where his 1994 debut full-length, “Critical Stage,” marked a turning point for the project. A second album, “Stored Images,” followed in 1995 and included one of Van Roy’s most enduring songs, “See You in Hell.” Van Roy co-founded the Dependent label in 1999, releasing “Mindstrip” in 2000, which reached number one on the German alternative chart, alongside the singles “Hellraiser” and “Comatose Delusion.” The 2003 album “Axis of Evil” was voted album of the year by the Deutsche Alternative Charts, and 2006’s “Bind, Torture, Kill” reached the top of the same chart on the strength of the single “Godsend + Menschenfresser.” In 2009, Van Roy signed Suicide Commando to Out of Line Music, releasing the 7″ “Severed Head / Until We Die” followed by the EP “Die Motherfucker Die,” which also topped the German alternative chart. “Implements of Hell” followed in 2010, then “When Evil Speaks” in 2013, “Forest of the Impaled” in 2017 and “Goddestruktor” in 2022, which reached number 9 on the official German album charts. For live performances, Van Roy is joined by Torben Schmidt on keyboards and Mario Vaerewijck on drums. “Destroyer of Worlds (SGNLS Version),” released as Suicide Commando marks its 40th anniversary, continues the project’s recent run of anniversary-focused releases alongside “Collective Suicide Vol. 1+2.”

items.body: KMFDM released the single “Enemy (Inhalt Geld ’88 Remix)” on Metropolis Records on 7 August 2026. The single reworks the title track of the industrial rock band’s album “Enemy,” released in February 2026, and is streaming via ffm.to/mqxraqy and on Bandcamp. Enemy (Inhalt Geld ’88 Remix) by KMFDM The remix comes from producer Matia Simovich, who records as Inhalt and owns Infinite Power Studios in Los Angeles. Simovich has previously worked as co-writer and/or producer with Peter Baumann of Tangerine Dream, Boy Harsher, Nitzer Ebb, Patriarchy and Madeline Goldstein. “KMFDM were a teenage instruction manual on how to arrange a song and subvert the status quo, all packaged under an ultra heavy beat,” Simovich stated. On the remix itself, Simovich commented: “I spent a whirlwind week putting the original song to the dancefloor, aided by an amazing polyphonic modular synthesizer but mixing to analog tape. I hope this remix lands with KMFDM fans new and old. It’s part dubby in the ‘UAIOE’ way, part Zappa in the ‘MONEY’ way, but all KMFDM attitude under the INHALT lens.” The comparisons reference KMFDM’s 1989 album “UAIÖE” and 1992 album “Money.” “Enemy (Inhalt Geld ’88 Remix)” is Simovich’s second KMFDM rework. He previously remixed the album track “Yoü” as “Yoü (Inhalt Kunst ’93 Remix),” released in April 2026 and streaming at ffm.to/youmix. The “Enemy” album was previewed with the songs “Oubliette” and its title track as singles and received positive reviews on release. About KMFDM KMFDM began in Paris in 1984 as a performance art project between Sascha Konietzko and German multimedia artist Udo Sturm. Konietzko, joined by drummer En Esch and vocalist Raymond Watts, recorded the band’s earliest material in Germany before relocating to Chicago, where KMFDM signed to the industrial label Wax Trax! Records and built its reputation through the late 1980s and 1990s with albums including “UAIÖE” (1989) and “Money” (1992). Konietzko is the only member to appear on every KMFDM release. Vocalist Lucia Cifarelli, Konietzko’s wife, joined the band’s lineup around the turn of the 2000s, and KMFDM has released through Metropolis Records for its more recent output. The band’s current lineup features Konietzko, Cifarelli and drummer Andy Selway, with contributions from Tidor Nieddu and Annabella Konietzko – daughter of Sascha Konietzko and Lucia Cifarelli – on the “Enemy” album. “Enemy,” released in February 2026, was followed by the “Yoü (Inhalt Kunst ’93 Remix)” single in April 2026 and now by “Enemy (Inhalt Geld ’88 Remix)” in August 2026, both reworked by producer Matia Simovich (Inhalt).

items.body: Minneapolis-based post-industrial artist EbE404 will release its third full-length album, “Cortisol,” on CD and digital August 21, 2026 via GIVE/TAKE. Pre-orders open August 7, 2026. The album comprises nine long-form drone, noise and power ambient pieces and follows the maxi-single “Flora,” due July 31, 2026 on the same label. ‘Cortisol’ unfolds across nine tracks “Cortisol” is described by GIVE/TAKE as a statement on the attention economy, built from reverb-soaked, multi-layered atmospheres and minimal rhythmic elements. EbE404 applies spatial mixing, interacting frequencies and phase manipulation across the record’s nine tracks. The label points to the project’s 2020 debut, “Tedium and Loss,” as a reference point for the album’s dark ambient tone. The label also states the release will not appear on Spotify, citing anti-AI marketing methods built around direct human sharing rather than algorithmic platforms. EbE404 describes the album directly: “This album is the sound of living through fascism, the worst people in the world, the execution of empathy, and a life being shaped by algorithms and a digital universe that is utterly detached from the real world – the inevitable result of The Attention Economy. Cortisol is the stress hormone, and this work traces the rise and fall of it as one meanders between virtual and structural nightmares while finding moments of distraction and respite. Feeling the unprecedented becoming normal and fighting to remain anchored in the real to avoid desensitization. Minneapolis has been a strange place to make art in this era, and this captures the horrors and hope of fighting back. This is for The Rebel Loons.” GIVE/TAKE lists reference points including Coil’s “Constant Shallowness Leads to Evil” era and Throbbing Gristle’s “Third Mind Movement” era. A Bandcamp listening party with EbE404 is set for release day, August 21, 2026 at 7 p.m. CST. About EbE404 EbE404 is a Minneapolis-based electronic project that keeps its members anonymous, working across post-industrial, dark ambient and IDM territory built around modular synthesis, Ableton Live sound design and field recordings. The project cites Coil, Nurse With Wound and Lustmord as reference points. EbE404 released its debut album, “Tedium and Loss,” on GIVE/TAKE on October 16, 2020. The second album, “Inrush,” followed on May 6, 2022; Side-Line spoke with EbE404 that year in a Click Interview, where the project described “Inrush” as a condensed 24-hour cycle exploring the patterns and routines of daily life. A remix album, “Ripple,” arrived August 19, 2022, followed by “Dark Ice Days” on July 21, 2023. “Cortisol,” set for August 21, 2026, arrives roughly three weeks after the maxi-single “Flora,” which previews the album with three versions of the track “Grass Time.” It is EbE404’s third full-length for GIVE/TAKE.

items.body: Belgian dark electro project Mildreda released a lyric video for “Silk Skin” on August 6, 2026, the latest advance single from the double album “Realities”, due August 28, 2026 on Dependent Records. “Silk Skin” opens the second disc of the release and follows earlier singles “End of the Line” and “Virtual Goddess”, the latter featuring Suicide Commando’s Johan Van Roy. ‘Silk Skin’: theme and production Mildreda mastermind Jan Dewulf wrote and produced “Silk Skin” around the tension between longing and retreat. “This track revolves around unspoken desires and the familiar, exhausting push and pull between longing and retreat,” Dewulf said. “I wanted to transform that tension into a ritual – a feverish invocation, a dance that binds, summons, and slowly pulls you under. Musically, the heavy bass was a happy accident in the studio, one that instantly revealed the direction that I needed to take. A relentless pulse rooted in EBM, and unmistakably Belgian at its sonic core.” Dewulf recorded, produced and mixed “Silk Skin” at Cyberflesh Loft in Ostend, with mastering by Pieter De Wagter at Equus in Vlezenbeek. The single has been cleared for immediate radio broadcast, and cover art and layout for “Realities” are by Henk Willems. About Mildreda Mildreda is the dark electro project of Belgian musician Jan Dewulf, who also records as Diskonnekted. Dewulf began Mildreda in the mid-1990s, drawn to the electronic body music of Belgian acts such as The Klinik, before setting the project aside to found Diskonnekted. He revived Mildreda in the 2010s, signing to Dependent Records and releasing “I Was Never Really There” in 2021 and the concept album “Blue-Devilled” in 2023. Christophe Salvatore plays live keyboards in the current line-up. The double album “Realities” follows “Blue-Devilled” as an 18-track, two-CD release on Dependent Records, featuring guest vocals from Suicide Commando‘s Johan Van Roy on “Virtual Goddess” and Constantin “Breñal” Warter of Calva Y Nada on “Rückwärts”. “Silk Skin” is the album’s latest preview ahead of its August 28, 2026 release.

The group has further festival dates confirmed at M’era Luna Festival in Hildesheim and Summer Breeze Open Air, both in Germany, ahead of a headline European tour across the UK, France, Germany and Czechia in October and November 2026. items.body: Stockholm post-punk trio Then Comes Silence released the single “Judgement Day” on August 7, 2026, the first single from their upcoming eighth album, “Requiem Ballroom”, due in November via Metropolis Records. The track pairs gothic rock guitar with what the band’s label calls “an unexpected Euro-techno pulse.” Judgement Day by Then Comes Silence ‘Judgement Day’: a Killing Joke homage Then Comes Silence founder Alex Svenson wrote “Judgement Day” as a tribute to Killing Joke, one of the band’s key influences. “‘Judgement Day’ was the first song I wrote for this album – an homage to our musical heroes Killing Joke. Hugo came up with the guitar sound early in the process. This song celebrates the wicked ones having a good run til their end days. In some people’s eyes, we too are rock ‘n’ rolling, beer drinking geezers that most likely will be the first to go. So be it. We had a good run,” Svenson said. Guitarist Hugo Zombie described the track’s sound and its live premiere: “The guitar is inspired by Killing Joke and is a little tribute to Geordie. We haven’t played it live, but we will perform it for the first time at M’era Luna Festival in August. It should go well.” The band shot a music video for “Judgement Day” in a photo studio. “We gave a performance in the photo studio when shooting the music video. It was like a regular concert with the extras dancing around the band. People seemed to enjoy being involved in the making of this video – it’s easy to dance to and has a good dynamic,” Svenson said. Drummer Jonas Fransson added a detail from the shoot: “We invited a bunch of friends to join us for the music video shoot, and one of them happens to be a 16-year-old Miniature Pinscher. He is almost completely deaf, so he didn’t mind walking around the studio while we were playing.” ‘Requiem Ballroom’: eighth album on Metropolis Records “Requiem Ballroom” is Then Comes Silence’s eighth album and follows 2024’s Trickery. Lyrics and music are by Alex Svenson, with additional synths from Johan Lange of Agent Side Grinder on one track. The album was recorded by Jörgen Wall and Tom van Heesch; the “Ballroom” half was mixed by Jon Bordon, and the “Requiem” half by Tom van Heesch, known for his work with Rammstein and Apocalyptica. Svante Forsbäck mastered the record at Chartmakers. The cover art is by D.K. Griftegaard and Jonas Fransson, and the “Judgement Day” video was directed by Damon Zurawski. items.body: It had been five years since the Spanish Dark-Electro project Asseptic Room released its previous album. Carlos Ruiz—formerly active as Dioxyde—and his companion Mario González now return with 16 new tracks that make up this fourth official album. Asseptic Room remains firmly rooted in dark, gloomy Electro, but this time the atmosphere takes center stage more than ever before. The songwriting is exceptionally detailed, yet the album’s greatest strength lies in the overwhelming sense of atmosphere it creates. At times, it even feels like the Soundtrack to a dark, dystopian film—Cinematic Dark-Electro would be a fitting description. The music is tormented and intense, driven by raw vocals delivered in both Spanish and English. Industrial elements occasionally emerge, adding extra power and texture to the already dark soundscape. Towards the end of the album, the music gradually becomes harder and more dancefloor-oriented. Personally, I still consider this to be the band’s strongest side, although that is, of course, a matter of taste. In any case, “Deconstructor” comes highly recommended for anyone with a passion for extremely Dark-Electro. The album may have flown somewhat under the radar, but it is certainly well worth discovering. (Rating:8). Listen to “Shame And Forgiveness”: Shame And Forgivness by Asseptic Room About Asseptic Room Asseptic Room is the Spanish dark electro project of Carlos Ruiz, who started as a DJ in Madrid in the late 1980s before forming Dioxyde with Marcos Calvo in 1998, releasing the debut album “Torschlusspanik”. Ruiz left Dioxyde in 2004 and founded Asseptic Room, releasing the albums “Morbid Visions” in 2006 and “Visceralofobia” in 2011 via Advoxya Records. Mario González joined the project, and the pair released the double album “Extinction Or Reawaken” via Advoxya Records. “Deconstructor” is Asseptic Room’s fourth official album, also released via Advoxya Records, arriving five years after its predecessor.

items.body: 会期：2026/04/25～2026/09/06 会場：金沢21世紀美術館［石川県］ 公式サイト：https://www.kanazawa21.jp/data_list.php?g=65&d=1852 （中編より） 前編の末尾で指摘したように、「路上、お邪魔ですか？」展における根本的な問題は、2020年に渋谷で起きた路上生活者殺害事件の加害者が発した「 彼女・・が邪魔だった」という言葉をタイトルに参照しつつも、展示内容において「ホームレスの女性」が透明化・排除され、ジェンダーの視点から「路上」を考える視点がまったく欠落していることにある。不特定多数の人々が行き交う路上は、ジェンダーにおいて決してニュートラルな空間ではない。むしろ、どのようなジェンダー（と見なされる）かによって、誰からどのような眼差しを向けられるのか（性的欲望なのか無関心なのか警戒なのか蔑視なのか）という経験がまったく異なり、それに付随して「路上を歩くこと」の安全度も危険度も異なってくる。つまり本展は、「路上、お邪魔ですか？」と掲げているが、路上で実際に「お前は邪魔だ」と 排除されない・・・・・・人の視線で企画されている。 「ホームレスの女性」という何重にも周縁化された存在に言及する現代美術作品が、まったく存在しないわけではない。例えば、2003年より東京都内の公園のブルーテント村に住み、2007年にホームレスの女性たちのグループ「ノラ」を立ち上げたいちむらみさこは、自身の日常生活と制作を地続きとしながら、ジェンダー、貧困、ジェントリフィケーションの問題に取り組んでいる★1。「Family」シリーズ（2013）では、テント村、近代異性愛家族や家父長制を象徴する「家」、家の内部にある墓、女性の身体、燃える炎などが赤い絵具で描かれたドローイングとともに、路上の映像が投影される★2。 以下では、本展出品作以外の作品や複数の論考を参照し、歴史的視座を交えて、ジェンダーやセクシュアリティの視点から「路上を歩くこと」の制約と権利について考える。フェミニズム美術史家グリゼルダ・ポロックは、古典的著作『視線と差異 フェミニズムで読む美術史』所収の論考「女性性（フェミニニティ）の空間とモダニティ」において、マネや印象派の男性画家と、ベルト・モリゾとメアリー・カサットという二人の印象派の女性画家が描いた「空間」の差異を分析することで、モダニティが、性と階級を二重に分離する複雑な政治的力学によって駆動していることを指摘した★3。モリゾとカサットの絵画に多く描かれたのは、食堂、客間、寝室、バルコニー、庭など、女性に割り当てられた家庭内の私的な空間である（モデルも家族や友人、使用人など私的な関係にある女性たちが多い）。家庭外の公的な空間を描いた作品もあるが、公園の散歩や劇場での観劇など、ブルジョワ階級が余暇を誇示する社交の空間に限定される。また、ポロックは、モリゾ作品では、欄干、バルコニー、堤防といった境界線によって、ひとつの画面が二つの空間体系に分離されるとともに、絵のなかの女性たちが「境界線の内側」の私的領域に閉じ込められていることに着目する。つまり、欄干やバルコニーは、公的空間と私的空間の境界に加え、男性性の空間と女性性の空間の境界でもあるという二重の象徴性を帯びている。 一方、マネや印象派の男性画家たちは、バーやカフェ、キャバレーという歓楽の場や、劇場の舞台裏、娼館すなわち金銭を介した性的交換の場に自由に出入りし、描くことができた。だが、ブルジョワ階級の女性がこうした場所へ立ち入ることは「品位を汚す行為」として禁止され、夫や付き添いの女性を伴わずにひとりで外出することも（娼婦と見なされるという）危険を伴い、不道徳な行為とみなされた。したがって、ヴァルター・ベンヤミンが『パサージュ論』で描いた、群衆のなかをそぞろ歩き、近代都市のスペクタクルな消費空間を心ゆくまで眺める「遊歩者」とは、男性に限定されたモデルであるとポロックは指摘する。つまり、モダニティとは、公私の領域を男性性と女性性に割り当てたうえで、処女／娼婦、子どもを産む女／性的欲望の対象としての女という二極のセクシュアリティに女性を分離して階級化する、性と階級が複雑に絡み合う政治的力学に支えられている。 だが、ポロック自身「モダニティはまだわれわれとともにある」と述べるように、こうした支配構造は過去のものではない。「女性性の空間はいまも女の生活を規制し、その規制は、街中で無遠慮な男の視線の攻撃を浴びることから卑劣な強姦までさまざまである」★4。この事例として、ローリー・アンダーソンの《Fully Automated Nikon（Object / Objection / Objectivity）》（1973）が挙げられる★5。アンダーソンは、フルオートのカメラの機動性を活かし、路上で性的なからかい目的で声をかけてきた男性を撮影し、状況を綴ったテクストを添えて展示した。「写真とテクスト」というコンセプチュアル・アートの王道を踏襲しつつ、見る／見られるというジェンダーの非対称性を転倒させ、女性の身体が客体化（Object）されることに対する異議申し立て（Objection）を痛烈に行なっている。また、被写体の男性の「目」に白いテープを貼って隠す操作も多義的な批評性を示す。「プライバシーの配慮」を装いつつ、「ちょっとしたいたずら」ではなく「犯罪」であると明示し、さらに彼を「匿名化」することで、こうした性犯罪がいたるところで無数に行なわれている遍在性をも示唆する。そして、「見られる対象」に置かれた男性は、女性の身体を無遠慮に眺めまわす有害な視線をも封じられているのだ。 最後に、「路上を安全に歩くこと」の権利は（シスジェンダーの）女性だけの問題に限らないこと、そして「歩く行為」が安全性の保障に加えて、連帯の可能性に開かれていることについて、哲学者・クィア理論家のジュディス・バトラーの論考を参照して考えたい。路上を歩く行為は、抗議活動に加えて、社会から不可視化された存在が「ここにいる」ことを自らの実存をもって示すための切実な手段でもある。だが、セクシュアル・マイノリティは、プライドパレードという祝祭的で非日常的な瞬間 にだけ ・・・ 、路上空間に姿を現わすわけではない。とりわけトランスジェンダーは、公共空間を歩くだけで、好奇や侮蔑の視線をジロジロと無遠慮に向けられ、侮蔑的な言葉を見知らぬ他人から浴びせられ、ときには身体的な暴力を受ける。言い換えれば、トランスジェンダーが公共空間を（精神的にも）安全に歩けるかどうかは、単にそのトランス個人の問題ではなく、同じ場所を歩いている人が「トランスが安全に歩ける権利を支持している」と表明しているかどうかにかかっている。バトラーは、『アセンブリ: 行為遂行性・複数性・政治』において、次のように述べる。 日常生活そのものが暴力の恐怖なしで成立し、保護されていなくても安全に歩けるようになるとすれば、間違いなくそれは、たとえその権利がたった一人によって行使される場合でさえ、多くの人々がその権利を支持しているからだ。（中略）歩くことは、ここはトランスジェンダーの人々が歩く公共空間である、ここは様々な形式の衣服を身にまとった人々が、どのようにジェンダー化されていようと、あるいはどの宗教を表明していようと、暴力に脅えることなく自由に移動できる公共空間である、と述べることなのである★6。 デモやパレードといった一時的で非日常的な行為に限らず、「歩くこと」は、特定の誰かを 排除しない ・・・・・ という姿勢を無言のうちに、自らの身体を通して日常的に示す連帯の行為にもなりうる。政治と日常性は矛盾しない。むしろ、日常的な歩行の行為のうちにも、政治性や連帯の意思は宿るのだ、という気づきこそが求められている。 ★1──いちむらみさこ『ホームレスでいること 見えるものと見えないもののあいだ』（創元社、2024） ★2──吉岡恵美子・伊藤まゆみ編『越境 : 収蔵作品とゲストアーティストがひらく視座 : 京都精華大学ギャラリーリニューアル記念展』（京都精華大学、2022） ★3──グリゼルダ・ポロック『視線と差異 フェミニズムで読む美術史』（萩原弘子訳、ちくま学芸文庫、2025、pp.151-232） ★4──同上、p.230 ★5──村上由鶴『アートとフェミニズムは誰のもの？』（光文社、2023、pp.219-223）。ヘレナ・レキット編、ペギー・フェラン概説『アート&フェミニズム』（鈴木奈々訳、ファイドン、2005、p.96） ★6──ジュディス・バトラー『アセンブリ : 行為遂行性・複数性・政治』（佐藤嘉幸・清水知子訳、青土社、2018、pp.69-70）。なお、引用箇所の訳の太字部分は下記を参照した。山田秀頌「バトラーとトランスの両義的な関係」（『現代思想』2019年3月臨時増刊号、pp.192-205） 鑑賞日：2026/06/20（土） 関連レビュー items.excerpt: 京都芸術センターにて、公募プログラム「Co-program」から派生した展覧会企画「Co-program Reframed ：飛光、飛光」が開催されています。 本展は、2025年度の公募において惜しくも採択とならなかった企画を再編し紹介する取り組みです。参加アーティストの今宿未悠、中澤ふくみ+花形槙+安田伸裕、藤田一樹は、いずれも身体を起点とした表現に取り組んでいます。 欠如や過剰を抱え、決して必要十分にはならない「私」という存在を起点に、それぞれの表現を通じて、社会や世界とのつながりを模索し続ける手立てについて思いを馳せる展覧会です。 開催プログラム ■藤田一樹パフォーマンス 日時｜2026/08/15（土）、08/16（日）、08/21（金）、08/22（土）各日16:00～ 会場｜京都芸術センター ミーティングルーム2 参加費｜1,000円 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください。 ■Extra Limb Circuit ／余剰肢回路 リハビリテーション 日時｜2026/08/22（土）14:00～17:00 会場｜京都芸術センター ギャラリー南 参加費｜無料 ＊詳細はこちらをご覧ください
